maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend suggests that once you open the door, once you exercise the authority of Parliament to determine the representation outside the provisions of section 51 generally, there is no limitation to the extent to which * that right might be exercised and no limitation to the number of representatives which might be given to each province. If you come to exercise the right conferred by section 52 of the Act of increasing the number of representatives generally, whatever power may be inferred from that particular clause can only be exer-



cried under and by virtue of the powers conferred by section 51. It has always seemed to me an anomaly, with the greatest possible deference to the distinguished public men on both sides of the House who, on previous occasions, have taken the position to refer to the provinces of the Dominion the question of considering the amendment of this representation question. There is no more argument, either from constitutional reasons or practice, why you should summon the representatives of the different provinces of the Dominion to consider the question of remodelling section 51 of the British North America Act than that you should summon them when you want to have legislation which might be deemed to be an extreme exercise of the federal power so far as the provisions of section 91 of the Act are concerned. In 1867, by virtue of the Imperial Act, there was committed .solely and entirely to this federal Parliament the duty of determining this -question of representation, and if we are to follow the view which has -been lately taken by Lord Haldane, in an Australian case, only a month ago, as to the method in which the Canadian constitution should be interpreted, a view which in some degrees, so far as the Privy Council is concerned, is a novel one in that he declares categorically and definitely that the constitution of Canada is not a federal constitution in the proper sense of the term not as the Australian constitution is, the absolute power of dealing with the whole -question of representation was committed to this federal Parliament; and the provinces and provincial Governments have nothing whatever to do with it except on the most theoretical principle. If you apply that theoretical principle in regard to section 51 of the British North America Act you must apply it to every other section where the exercise of powers by the federal Government is provided for. Why do I make that proposition? For this reason, that I wish to make a suggestion to my right hon. friend that if he desires to help the smaller provinces of the Dominion-and I am free to -say that I believe he does,-an opportunity arises for him to do so because of the anomaly in regard to representation which arises in connection with this province of Prince Edward Island, to which he referred the other day. By the provisions of this Bill, the province of Prince Edward Island will have
three representatives in this House, while it has four representatives in the Senate. New Brunswick will have eleven representatives here, while it has ten representatives in the Senate, and it is not too violent a presumption to make that perhaps at a very early date there may arise conditions under which that representation may -still further be reduced. You would then have a condition under which these smaller provinces would have a l-arger representation in the Senate than in the popular branch. That is certainly an anomaly which was never contemplated by the fathers of Confederation or by the leading men of those smaller provinces when they gave up their individual identity in order to become merged in the greater federation. It seems to me. that if my right hon. friend is really desirous of assisting the smaller provinces, he should proceed in the only method in which he can legally proceed, by moving an Address to the Imperial P-a-rl-iament, asking them to amend the British North America Act, so that for any province of the Dominion of Canada there shall not be, at any time, a less number of representatives in the popular branch than in the Senate. I think that is a proposition which would not be unfair or unreasonable, and having regard to the many considerations which might be urged on behalf of the smaller provinces, it seems to me to be a* proposition which -might very well receive the approbation of the whole House. I have- dealt at some length on this point because I contend that Parliament should not send out to this committee the task of dealing with this question of representation in any elastic or uncertain way, so far as the question of numbers is concerned. The status of that committee, their powers, and their limitations should be definitely recognized by th-is House, and at this stage, so that there may not be any attempt by the committee to exercise any unconstitutional power or to proceed beyond their authority in dealing -wit'll this question.
My right hon. friend was good enough to refer to a question to which I called his attention on the introduction of the Bill, when I was unable to plaee fairly before the House a point that is held by a good number of hon. gentlemen here and by quite a number outside the Ho use to be an important one; that is, in regard to subsection 4 of section 51. My right hon. friend has answered the point which was raised at that time. The popular view in regard to subsection 4 is that the clause was to apply only in cases where there had been a certain

percentage oi reduction in population. The percentage contemplated by the state is one intended to be made between two fractions, the numerator of the fraction being the population of a particular province ten years ago and the denominator being the population of the Dominion at that time. You take similar fractions for the last census and you make a comparison between the two; the question then is, whether or not that section is to be interpreted by ascertaining whether the difference between these two fractions is less than a fraction of one-twentieth, or whether it is less than one-twentieth of what the original fraction was. That may seem a little complicated, but that is the way in which one would put the question as a matter of accuracy. After deliberation I am inclined to agree with the interpretation put upon this by my right hon. friend. In ordinary language the subsection reads, unless the difference between these two fractions is ascertained at the then latest census, to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upward. Does that mean one-twentieth part of the fraction which	was	made	by	a comparison made with the population of the province ten years ago, or is it the fraction, one-twentieth, without relation to that? I am inclined to say that I agree with the right hon. gentleman in the view he takes of it. I submitted [DOT] the proposition because the suggestion had been made to me by a gentleman of another chamber who felt this question of representation, its reduction and	the	status	of	the smallerprovinces-as	all	must	feel	who giveany thought	at	all to	the	matter-to
' be of very great importance. So much for that phase of the question, but I submit that we should have from the Minister of Justice who is the official adviser upon these questions, a statement as to whether or not he agrees with the view put forward by my right hon. friend and leader, in regard to the power Parliament has to interfere with the scale of representation definitely and positively laid down under section 51 of the Act. My right hon. friend in introducing this Bill, outlined certain principles which he thought should guide the committee, and as the House after this second reading will have heard the last of this question of representation until that committee reports, I think the lines upon which they should act with regard to matters of policy should be very carefully considered. The Prime Minister mentioned that the committee which dealt with 54*
this question in England were affected by certain considerations: first, equality of population; secondly representation in borough divisions of a population of an urban character; thirdly, compactness in respect of geographical position and fourthly community of interests, and in suggesting to this committee what their motive should be in dealing with this question, he suggested that they should have before them, first, the observance of municipal boundaries. That idea is one which has been accentuated by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, and although in times gone by battles waged in this House around the question of municipal boundaries, it is gratifying to-day to know that both parties have come to realize the importance and necessity of having regard to municipal boundaries when delimiting constituencies for the federal Parliament. The second principle which he thought should be regarded, was that of equality of population which of course was one which had to be considered in connection with the observance of municipal boundaries; the third, a greater unit for city constituencies than for country constituencies without fixing any definite percentage and, fourth, a community of interests and geographical contiguity. The Prime Minister indicated that these suggestions come within what his views are to the lines within which the committee should act.
It seems to me that there are some considerations further than ' that which ought to be regarded. We should have regard to the permanence and stability of existing constituencies. Where you have a constituency in which men have resided for long periods of time, where their municipal interests are bound up together, where their business interests centre around certain villages or towns iD a particular community, and where, for a long period of time, public men on both sides have been wont to deal with the necessities and interests of a particular class of people, it seems to me that we should not lightly interfere with settled conditions of that kind. That proposition seems to be one the wisdom of which is so patent that I am quite sure the Prime Minister will agree with me as to its desirability.
But a difficulty will arise, as it always has arisen, in this way: Where, as a result of the increase in the population of existing constituencies additional members have to be provided for, how are you

going to proceed? Take the situation in the new provinces of the Northwest, where we have ten, and ten and seven members respectively? Take the two great provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta where the additional representation created by this Act will necessitate the breaking up of constituencies which are represented in this House by hon. gentlemen- On what principle are you to proceed in that particular? Where you do not have to interfere with the representation of any particular province by increase or diminution, where you have county boundaries and existing conditions, there is no special warrant for the committee undertaking to interfere with those conditions as far as representation is concerned unless there is some great disparity in the unit of representation with reference to a particular constituency. The discharge of such a task ought not to be a very great one, but when you come to deal with the problem of increased representation, where you have to take existing constituencies and break them up in order to provide for representation throughout the borders of a once great constituency represented by one member, on what principle are you going to proceed? In the Northwest, unfortunately, to-day, we have not municipal government throughout the rural districts. We have not, therefore, that guiding spirit of municipal institutions that we have in the eastern portion of Canada. It .seems to me that the prime consideration that ought to exist there in regard to the determination of the question is unity of interest and the geographical position of the new constituency as it is to be formed. There is no use in creating a constituency an indefinite number of miles in length, in which the people at one end never see the people at the other end from one year to another. What a farce it must be, as a matter of representation, for an hon. gentleman in this House to represent a constituency in which these principles of community of interest and geographical connection have been disregarded for some other considerations. I hope that the committee, in dealing with this question, will not be affected by political considerations, but will be guided by the lines laid down so well by the Prime Minister and by the leader of the Opposition.
Another principle arises where you have districts which are divided by stretches of water or other natural or geographical barriers which prevent a community of interest and that intimate connection

which one part of a constituency should have with another in order to have that proper touch between the representative and the people. I venture to point out that the situation that exists in our own province affords a particular exemplification of the principles that I want to deal with. There we have the island of Cape Breton which historically at one time had a separate existence from that of the province of Nova Scotia. It is not connected with the mainland in any way. A stretch of water runs between the Island of Cape Breton and what is called the mainland of the province of Nova Scotia. There we have had within the last fifteen years what might be called a displacement of population. The development of the steel and coal industries in that island has resulted to a very great degree in the farmers leaving their farms in the country, or the young men leaving the old people on the farms, and going off to work in these industrial centres. As a consequence the population of the island of Cape Breton has not been diminished. They have had four representatives in this House, and I would submit that there is an idea strongly held that as you have this natural barrier which prevents this island and its people from having direct communication with the mainland, the entity of the island of Caps Breton should be recognized and that the four representatives of that portion of the province should be maintained there. You can go to other portions of the Dominion where you find natural barriers and where it is not easy to divide one class of people from another. These should be arranged so that you would not have a mixed constituency in which one portion of it would have no interest whatever in the men who happened to live across the barrier. That proposition seems to me to be self-evident.
I was surprised that the right hon. Prime Minister did not state to the House that he was considering the question of proportionate representation. I do not propose to argue that question at very great length, but inasmuch as public men have from time to time during the last ten or fifteen years in this House and elsewhere discussed this important question, it seems to me that on the present occasion some pronouncement should have been made by the Prime Minister with regard to it. I invite the attention of the Prime Minister now to this matter.
I hope also that the Prime Minister will respond to the suggestion of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in

regard to increasing the numbers of the committee, not for any reason other than that I think the public interest would be served and that we would have better results. It might be urged that if you have nine members on the committee you are more apt to have complicated questions arise than if you have only seven. I recall that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister ten years ago suggested to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that the committee should be made up of four from each side of the House, which would have made the membership of the committee eight. The request of the leader of the Opposition to make it nine seems to me a natural one in view of the fact that we have in these two new provinces and in the country extending from the Great Lakes to the Pacific Ocean, a body of men interested in this country whose representation in this Parliament will exceed the representation that some of the provinces of the Dominion had at Confederation and for some time afterwards, and will exceed what they now have.
In no spirit of contention, but simply with the idea that under such an arrangement this problem may be worked out upon the lines which I apprehend the Prime Minister would like to have it worked out upon, I have ventured to put forth these suggestions. If the committee is to partake of the nature of a conference with the idea of devising an equitable scheme of representation, then my right hon. friend will have an easy task in so far as representation problems are concerned in this Parliament. The ideal, I think, should be that the committee, in discharging their duties, should act as conferees. If, on the other hand, you are going to have this condition in the committee, that merely on account of the fact that you have a preponderance of members on the committee who are going to exercise their authority in regard to any hard and fast scheme, the whole object of the committee will be at once nullified.
The Prime Minister, on the motion for the first reading, declared his satisfaction wijh the methods pursued by the committee appointed ten years ago. If these rumours, which we hear now and then, as to the studious efforts of certain gentlemen in parcelling out constituencies in certain provinces of the Dominion, are correct, and if these gentlemen are to produce before the committee a hard and fast scheme, by which the considerations which
have been discussed on the first and second readings of this Bill are to be ignored, then I say to the Prime Minister that he can hardly expect that this committee can, in any sense, be called a combination of conferees in the public interest. Rather, it would degenerate into a combination in which the majority would rule, if they were permitted to rule. The Prime Minister himself, in dealing with this question, has approached the consideration of it in a very fair spirit, and has indicated the lines upon which the committee should act. I trust that spirit may be maintained.
A suggestion was made by the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) ten years ago, as to whether this committee should not have power to send for persons and papers. I do not know what form the resolution to be moved by my right hon. friend in regard to the appointment of the committee will take, but if the committee should proceed upon the lines of being conferees in the public interest, there may be no necessity for this special power .being delegated to the committee. Of course, hon. gentlemen on this side of the House should reserve the right to come to Parliament and ask that this power be granted should occasion arise.
It is to be hoped that in dealing with this question the policy which was inaugurated ten years ago-a policy which has been followed to a wider extent in England-will dominate the deliberations of the committee to which this Bill is to be referred. The party advantage which may momentarily be obtained by an unfair redistribution is one which ultimately does not bring that satisfaction or that result which men in public life should aim at. We on this side of the House, as our right hon. leader has said, hope that the Government will implement, in the appointment of the committee, and in the conduct of its deliberations, the generous assurances which the right hon. the Prime Minister has given us in moving the first and second readings of the Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. HUGHES (Prince Edward Island):
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
There is no doubt whatever that the delegates from Prince Edward Island who negotiated the terms upon which the Island came into Confederation, were convinced that they were getting for that province in this House of Commons six representatives for all time to come. There is equally no doubt, that the sub-committee of the Privy Council, with which they

negotiated these terms, were under the same impression. An examination of the Confederation documents and of the negotiations at that time, will convince any person of the fact as I state it. I am satisfied that the Prime Minister recognizes this fact, and I am satified also that several members of this House are equally convinced. Unfortunately that provision was not put in the terms of Union, and so we have to abide by the British North America Act as it exists. If the purpose of the Prime Minister in leaving the Prince Edward Island Schedule in the Bill blank in the reference to the committee, is because he thinks the committee is a better body than this House to examine the documents and to come to u decision, and if, should the committee recommend, after consideration of the matter, that Prince Edward Island should have four or six representatives, it is the intention of the right hon. gentleman to petition the home Government to so amend the British North America Act, then I can understand his course in thus referring the matter to the committee. But, if on the other hand, the committee should make such a recommendation, and the right hon. gentleman does not intend to carry it out, then I can hardly give the Prime Minister credit for sincerity. However, I will take the more honourable view, and I will suppose that the object of the Prime Minister in submitting this matter to the committee as he proposes, is to take the necessary steps to carry out the recommendation of the committee, in this respect, if such recommendation should be made.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The committee may or may not find it necessary to look into these matters to which my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) has referred, but I would like to point out to him that I have tried to find in ' Hansard ' any record of protest from gentlemen representing Prince Edward Island on the two former occasions When the representation of that province in this House was reduced. I may not have covered the whole ground in my search, but so far I [DOT]have not been able to find any such protest. If there has been any such protest in this House on these former occasions, it might be well to place it before the committee. If there was no protest, why was there not a protest?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
As I understand it, when the first reduction was made in accordance with the census of 1891, Sir John Thompson, then Minister of Justice,

gave it as his opinion that under the British North America Act, the provisions of Which would have to be carried out, Prince Edward Island would have to lose a member. Several eminent jurists have given expression to a similar opinion. The province brought its case before the Supreme Court of Canada, and afterwards before the Privy Council, and the decision was against the contention of the province. If no protest was entered, I presume it was because of that. However, on two different occasions in this House, once when a petition was going to the home Government to have the British North America Act amended with regard to the increased subsidies to the provinces, I thought it a good time to have this amendment made, if it were to be at all, and I presented my views to the House, and the hon. gentleman will find them in ' Hansard.' I presented the case then, and I need not go over the arguments now. I thought I made out a fairly good case, that the intention of both parties to the terms of union when the province of Prince Edward Island came in was that it should have a fixed number of six members. We stayed out of Confederation for six years on that point. Finally we came in. I have not the arguments here, but they can be easily obtained.
There is another matter to which I wish to refer briefly. It affects myself in a personal way to a great extent. When the Prime Minister introduced this Bill on the 10th of this month, he stated that the hon. member for Kings-that is myself-in 1903 had argued both strongly and forcibly against claims put forward by Prince Edward Island with respect to representation. I was somewhat surprised to hear the Prime Minister make such a statement, because I had no recollection of ever having done so, and I could not find in ' Hansard ' of 1903 where I had done so. I asked him to point out the place in ' Hansard ' Yesterday, before the Orders of the Day were called, he told me that I would find my remarks to which he had referred on page 10,909 of ' Hansard ' of 1903. In order that we may clear up this question, I think I had better read the statement that the Prime Minister made in reference to myself when he introduced this Bill. This was the paragraph in his speech:
It has been noted that in 1882 the Redistribution Bill did not diminish the representation of the province of Prince Edward Island, although according to the census of 1881, Prince Edward Island was at that time entitled to no more than five members. At first I was very much impressed by this circumstance, but I

observed that in a speech made by the hon. member for Kings, Prince Edward Island,^ in 1903, who argued strongly and forcibly against the claims put forward on behalf of the province at that time, he attributed this result to the fact that there was no previous census with which the census of 1381 could be compared for the purposes of subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, and probably that accounts for the result in 1882.
I would gather from that, that the Prime Minister stated really that he did not apprehend the meaning of subsection 4 of section 51 as fully as myself. Of course, that is a very high compliment for the right hon. gentleman to pay me, because I am not at all learned in the law, and I always understood that my right hon. friend was a distinguished member of the Bar. However, if he wishes to pay me that compliment, I will accept it and I can only say this, that there are many subjects on which I am much better informed than I am on legal questions, and I would be glad to give my hon. friend information at any other time on any other subject. I have turned up page 10,909 of ' Hansard ' of 1903, and I find that my speech on that occasion was very short, exactly one page of ' Hansard.' Mr. Hackett, the member for West Prince, P.E.I., had been speaking and had pointed out that in 1882 the Government led by the Right Hon. Sir John Macdonald had not decreased the representation of Prince Edward Island, although according to population it was entitled to no more than five members at that time, whereas it had six. He said that Sir John Macdonald was entitled, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned, to a great deal of gratitude for not decreasing the representation. He also stated that this Parliament had the power to give Prince Edward Island its original representation of six members. That was an extraordinary statement to make. Although I was not learned in the law, I knew that this Parliament had no power to give to Prince Edward Island six members or any more than it was entitled to under the provisions of the British North America Act. As my statement was very short, I will read it so that there will be no misunderstanding as to what I said in regard to the matter. This is what I said:
I have listened with some surprise to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett), in view of the fact that some ten years ago, when the last Redistribution Bill was under consideration and when the representation of Prince Edward Island was first reduced, my hon. friend and his political associates in Prince Edward
Island did not raise a solitary objection. At that time there were two Conservative representatives from the county of Kings in this House, and neither of them raised any objection. My hon. friend at thac time, though not a member of this House, was an influential man in the riding which he now represents and took an active part in politics. At that time not a meeting was held in the hon. gentleman's constituency, net a resolution was passed, no objection was raised, no protest was entered against the reduction of the representation of Prince Edward Island. Now, why bring it up at this late date? In my opinion, the proper time to enter a protest was when the representation was first reduced. But the hon. gentleman's political friends were then in power, and perhaps it was not thought to be good, political tactics to briflg up the question at that time.
As I listened to the hon. gentleman's remarks this evening, I could not help thinking what an opportunity he lost when he failed to go before the Supreme Court and argue the case of Prince Edward Island when this matter was submitted to it for decision. He made a strong argument here to-night, and it is a pity this argument was not presented when the Supreme Court was considering the case. If there had been any constitutional objection to my hon. friend appearing before the Supreme Court on account of being a layman, I am sure jf he had given his views to the counsel who was representing Prince Edward Island, that gentleman would have been very glad to present them before the court. The hon. gentleman says that in 1881 the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald allowed Prince Edward Island to retain its original representation, though the population of the province did not entitle it to to that representation. The reason of that was, I think, because the census of 1881 was the first Dominion census that was taken after the Island entered Confederation, and consequently there was no previous census with which to compare that one, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned. Therefore, no one could tell whether the twentieth part saving clause would protect the province against any reduction in its representation. That, I think, was the reason why the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald at that time did not reduce the representation, at all events, it would be a good and sufficient reason. But in 1891-92 when the next census was taken the representation of that province was reduced. At that time, I think, Sir John Thompson was leader of the Government-if not, he was Minister of Justice-and he declared there was nothing in the constitution to protect ithq province against a reduction in its representation. As I have already pointed out, the Conservative representatives in this House at thac time, the Conservative party and the press of Prince Edward Island-everybody acquiesced in the reduction that then took place. Therefore, I think it is altogether too late for my hon. friend and his political associates from Prince Edward Island to try to make political capital out of it at this time. We have to abide by the constitution under which we live.
I regret as much as any man can regret that the delegates at the time that the province of Prince Edward Island joined the union overlooked this important point, and did not provide against the contingency -that has since arisen. I also regret that a reduction has taken

place in the representation of the other Maritime provinces, because it will weaken the voice of those other provinces down by the sea to that extent in the great counsel of the nation.
In view of the fact that the highest constitutional authorities in Canada nave declared that the law affords the Maritime provinces no protection against a reduction of their representation, that there is nothing in the British North America Act that will preserve their original representation, I believe, however, that if the matter were properly presented to our friends from the other provinces they would agree to a change in the British North America Act providing that the representation in none of the provinces should be reduced beyond the representation they possessed when they originally entered Confederation. I believe that if the members from the other provinces would agree to that, it could be carried out, and possibly and probably that will be done before the next decennial revision takes place. That is the only way, in my judgment, that this matter can be accomplished. I cannot understand what my hon. friend had in view in bringing up this question to-night, unless it were to try to make political capital out of it. As I say, we have to bide by the constitution under which we live, and in view of the fact that this question has been argued before the highest court in Canada and decided against us, I am sure my hon. friend has sense enough to know that nothing he could say this evening would affect the issue in any way. He has merely brought up the matter again for the purpose of seeing it ventilated in Prince Edward Island, and giving the Conservative papers down there something to talk about, and an occasion to raise some objection to the present Administration.
Now, Sir, I have read every word that I uttered on that occasion, and I say that there is not a sentence, not a line, not a word, not a syllable in that speech to justify the right hon. Prime Minister in saying that I argued against the claims put forward by Prince Edward Island. Of course, under the circumstances, I believe the right hon. gentleman made a mistake and that the idea must have been suggested to him by somebody else. If he has read my speech, I am sure he will have come to the conclusion that there is nothing there to justify the charge he made against me. He has misrepresented me. And I would ask him, and expect him, to say that he was mistaken, or misinformed, and, as an honourable man and Prime Minister of this country, to withdraw the statement. That is due to his position.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I think we can all compliment the House on the fair way in which it has approached this measure. I shall ask for the attention of hon. members for only a minute or two to mention one or two points that, I think, should be stated, before the Bill goes to the committee. In the first place, I sympathize with what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. 
Macdonald) says about proportionate representation. I listened very carefully to what the former Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said with regard to municipal representation and preserving municipal bounds, but to my mind more important still is the representation of the minorities and of great classes that now are not represented. Proportional representation is now widely agitated and the system is well developed, but it has not quite found expression in our law. I do think that we should make the effort in the direction of proportional representation so as to secure the representation of minorities in this House. Take, for instance, the city of Toronto, where I live; we have now eight members for the city and the county of York. But there are substantial minorities in that city that are not represented here. There is a great labour vote in Toronto, yet Toronto does not send a labour representative to this House. A feature of representation in England is the strength of the labour representation in the House of Commons. If we had proportional representation recognized in this country-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What about the Liberal vote?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can deal with that. But perhaps proportional representation would secure some representation of the Liberals in this House, and, if so, the hon. gentleman should give me encouragement in this matter.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said there were important minorities not represented here, and I said that the Liberals of Toronto form one of those minorities.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Then, proportional representation would give them what they desire, and I should expect the Liberals to uphold that principle rather than the principle of municipal bounds. We should seek, not to give fair representation to municipalities, but to give fair representation to the political thought of the people.
As to this complaint of the smaller provinces as to reduction in their representation, if I had my way I would greatly reduce the number of members in this House, in the Senate and in our legislatures generally. I believe we should have better legislatures and a better Parliament if our numbers were smaller. While I regret that some of the provinces have to accept a reduction-Ontario being one of them-it becomes the duty of those provinces to im-

prove their representation if they possibly can. If the Maritime provinces wish to be strong in the Confederation-if I may be pardoned the suggestion-I think there ought to be a Maritime union into a single province. The Maritime provinces would be stronger in this House and in their influence in the country than they are to-day, divided into three provinces and with this question of representation, and especially this question of reduction in representation, coming up every ten years.
For forty-six years the experiment of Confederation has been going on, and it has succeeded in a remarkable degree.
But that constitution, which was written nearly fifty years ago, could not 5 p.m. foresee all the difficulties and circumstances that would develop. Probably the time has come, or will be here when our next Parliament sits, when Parliament should give attention to a constitutional revision to deal with the questions that have been widely discussed and that must be settled. Probably that would be the time when the smaller provinces could present their claims for better representation in this House. Certainly, the time will come when the Senate of this country must be reorganized. With the province of Prince Edward Island represented by four members in the Senate and only three here, it is clear that there is an unfair condition of things, and that unfairness should be removed. I trust that in the next Parliament some proposal for a conference of the provinces on the subject of constitutional revision will be made and a number of anomalies and grievances-and there are not many-will be removed, or at least an attempt made to remove them. I believe that when that takes place the smaller provinces can have any fair grievances brought before this Parliament and before the Imperial Parliament for cure-In the meantime it seems to me tliere is nothing to do but to respect the constitution and carry it out literally. The people of Ontario, as far as I can speak for that province, will stand for the reduction that is coming to them. The province has been greatly increased in its territory, yet the representation has to be reduced, and we abide loyally by the constitution as it should be carried out. We also are glad to see that the great provinces in the West are having that increased representation which is coming to them. If there is a place where proportional representation could be tried it is in the West. I do not say that
we could put it in force on this occasion but there is no reason why proportional representation should not be attempted in some constituencies, and in that way we might bring about what this law should bring about, a better representation of the political thought of the people, rather than a representation of people who seem to think [DOT]together municipally. That is no great bond in regard to politics. Our effort should be to get in this House a fair representation of the political thought of all the people of the country.
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) :	Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has followed the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) in the discussion of proportional representation. I am not sure but that there is a good deal in his contention. If I remember, a few years ago something of this kind was tried in Toronto but it was withdrawn.

There is a good deal to be said in favour of minorities being represented. As a matter of fact, the minorities under our system are not represented as they should be. A difference of one voter in a constituency may make an entire difference of the thought which the member pretends to represent. He comes here as representing the thought of the whole constituency, but he does not do anything of the kind. I am rather inclined to believe, with the member for Pictou and the member for York, that there is a great deal in the contention that proportional representation might be tried at least in a portion of Canada with no detrimental result to any one.
Mr. BURNHAM Has the hon. gentleman looked into the fact that there may be a variety of different opinions in any constituency, and if he is going to give representation to those opinions he might have not one but five or six candidates.

speechtext:
They would work out
their own salvation on that line whether they were one or ten. Generally speaking, the voters in a riding are divided largely into two classes and they culminate their

views in the discussions between the two great parties; but if there be some other wing of the people who have something else in their minds, 'they ought to be represented in this House; and under proportional representation it would be possible to work that out.
Now as to the question of the smaller provinces, I do not propose to speak* for Ontario, I am speaking now for myself. Possibly the members for Ontario may agree with me largely. The basis of our representation is supposed to be population. That decision was not arrived at without a good deal of discussion, thought and hard feelings on many sides; but finally the representation of the Dominion of Canada in this House is supposed to be by population, and to change that must be to change the foundation in that respect of the British Noith America Act. The Confederation itself was based on compromise. No country has ever achieved great success in any departure from existing conditions without both, schools of thought compromising to some extent, without, as we say, giving and taking. As Confederation was based on compromise, I would have no hesitation, if it could be worked out, either by a change of the British North America Act or otherwise, in allowing the smaller provinces to maintain their present representation, or even to have the representation which they had at the time of Confederation. This is not Prince Edward Island, [DOT] or Manitoba, or Quebec, or Ontario, Nova Scotia, -or New Brunswick; this is Canada, and what is best for Canada as a whole we, in each part of Canada, ought to try and work out, regardless of whether it harmonizes entirely with our own beliefs or not. But, coming back to representation, there is something wrong with our basis o-f representation, so far as minorities are concerned. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), the other night had a grievance from Quebec as to the number of me nbers in this House on each side. He contended that, according to the votes oast in 1911, there should be a difference of only one, thirty-two Conservatives and thirty-three Liberals; whereas there was quite a large discrepancy between the number of Conservatives and the number of Liberals returned to this House. I was struck with the figures and commenced figuring to see if the basis of the whole fabric of representation was not wrong. I took the Dominion of Canada and the vote cast in Canada in 1911. The total number of votes cast was 1,307,528. For

the Conservatives there were cast 669,594, and for the Liberals 625,103, and for the Independents 12,831. The difference in the Dominion of Canada between the votes cast for Conservatives and for Liberals was only 44,491-and that included Toronto. The average vote oast in each constituency was about 6,200. If we work that out as did the Postmaster General, in this House at the present time there should be 114 Conservatives and 107 Liberals, or a majority of just seven. That is worse than my hon. friend found in Quebec.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

speechtext:
I will give them to my hon. friend when the Bill comes back. As this redistribution is on the census of 1910 the figures before that would not be conducive to the enlightenment of the House.
Take my own province of Ontario-and it, I think, will show that the hon. member for South York is right in saying that minorities are not properly represented under the present system-and with such an injustice done to the Liberal party by a Liberal Government you can see that there must be something wrong with the system. I almost hesitate to trust ourselves even to that committee under that system. Take Ontario, the total vote oast was 480,572. Of these 269,930 were cast for Conservatives [DOT] and 207,078 for Liberals, a difference of 62,852. Let me see how it worked out. We have in this House 72 Conservatives and 14 Liberals. There was more difference than that before the South Bruce election, but at the present time it is 72 to 14. If we worked this out according to my hon. friend's figuring, there should be from Ontario 38 Liberals and 48 Conservatives, a difference of 10 instead of 58. I applied the figures of the Postmaster General for the whole of Canada to our own province to show that there must be something wrong with our system if it is not applicable to present-day conditions.
I recognize that the work of the committee will be arduous. There will be many differences of opinion, but I urge them-and I feel confident they will do it-to take all possible pains to see that, while county boundaries are maintained so far as possible, the people of the Dominion of Canada are given the right to be properly represented according to their views, and according to population, whether it be in condensed centers or rural districts.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. McLEAN (Queens, Prince Edward Island):
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I was pleased to hear the remarks of my hon. friend from South Renfrew with reference to the representation of the . Maritime provinces. I agree with him that, under present conditions, it would he proper for this Parliament to restore to the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island the representation which they had at Confederation. In 1864, when the first conference in regard to Confederation was held in Charlottetown, at which representatives of all the provinces were present, a programme was drawn up but was not agreed to at that time. The conference was adjourned to Quebec, and the programme again submitted, but the delegates from Prince Edward Island did not see fit to agree with the programme as regards their representation. It gave them only five representatives in a House of, I think, 194. They thought that they would lose all their influence if they agreed to any such programme, and in consequence they did not enter Confederation in 1867. The Dominion of Canada, in order to round out the Confederation, wanted Prince Edward Island to come in, but the Island held out for six members. Their population did not justify the Dominion granting them that number; it only justified the granting of five members. But at last, on the 9th of July, 1873, Prince Edward Island was granted six members and came into Confederation. The question of redistribution has been before Parliament on many occasions. The first redistribution was made in 1881, when Prince Edward Island, though only entitled to five members, was allowed to retain her six. I wish to impress this upon the House, because at that time it was well known that Prince Edward Island had not the population to justify the granting of six members. When my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes) made his address before this House in 1903, he made the statement attributed to him by the leader of the House:
The hon. gentleman says that in 1881 the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald allowed Prince Edward Island to retain its original representation, though the population of the province did not entitle it to that representation. The reason of that was, I think, because the census of 1881 was the first Dominion census that was taken after the Island entered Confederation, and consequently there was no previous census with which to compare that one, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned.
I think that was a lame excuse from the hon. member for Kings. He is a man
well informed on public affairs and when he made that speech in 1903 he knew well that a census was taken in Prince Edward Island in 1871 and that a report of that census was in the lit rary of this Parliament. He knew that, when he made the statement that there was no census of Prince Edward Island to compare with the Dominion census of 1881. He made a statement which he knew was not in accordance with the facts. The census of 1871 gave the papulation of Prince Edward Island as 93,698.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I was out of the
Chamber when my hon. friend was referring to me but I understand that the hon. gentleman has said there was a Dominion census before 1881. He must know that statement is incorrect.
Mr. A. A. MoLEAN:	I made no such
statement. I said that there was a census of Prince Edward Island before it entered Confederation; that the report of that census was in the library in 1903 when the hon. member made his speech, and that the report of that census could have been compared with the Dominion census of 1881. But instead of the hon. member getting that information from the library and giving it to the House, he found fault with the Conservative members who represented the province in the Parliament of 1881. In 1892, he also found fault with the manner in which the Prince Edward Island representatives conducted this busi-' ness of representation. At that time the province was very ably represented on the Liberal side. Sir Louis Davies represented one of our constituencies. He sat in this House during the discussion, but not one word was said by him, or by any other representative with regard to representation in Prince Edward Island. I do not know why, and I do not suppose the hon. member for Kings knows anything more about it than I do. No reflections need be cast on any one for having neglected to do his duty as a representative of Prince Edward Island at that time. After the Redistribution Act of 1892, the people of Prince Edward Island began to agitate for the restoration of their original representation, and in 1902 they forwarded a resolution, passed by the legislature of the province, to the Dominion Parliament protesting strongly against the reduction in representation. That resolution is to be found in the journals of the Prince Edward Island legislature. It placed the matter clearly before Parliament.

The resolution is a very long one. I do not intend to read it at the present time. I may have another opportunity of bringing the matter to the attention of the House before the debate closes. This resolution was moved by the Hon. Mr. Peters, at that time Premier, seconded by the Hon. Mr. Rogers, and adopted by the Legislature of Prince Edward Island. In it all the different stages by which Prince Edward Island was admitted into the Union are described. It sets forth that the terms and conditions upon which Prince Edward Island entered the Dominion of Canada were expressed in addresses from the legislature of the then colony, and amongst these conditions was the following:
That the population of Prince Edward Island having increased by 15,000 or upwards since the year 1861, the island shall be represented in the House of Commons of Canada by six members ;-	,
Here is a matter which should receive the consideration of this House when it is dealing with the representation of Prince Edward Island. Why was it that the number six was put into that address ? It was because the population of Prince Edward Island had increased by 15,000 or upwards since the year 1861.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What date was that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
the most she was entitled to during that period would be four members. And yet, Prince Ed.ward Island came into Confederation under the same moral agreement as did British Columbia. Then, when Manitoba came into Confederation, Manitoba was conceded four members when her population was less than one unit, entitling her at most to only one member. There was a further provision in the Manitoba Act that after the census of 1881 the representation of the province should be readusted under the terms of the British North America Act. The census of 1881 showed that Manitoba had a population of 62,260, which would have entitled her to three members, but in that redistribution Manitoba got five members and not three.
The question of the representation of Prince Edward Island has been before this House for a great number of years. It was discussed in 1903; and in 1905 and 1907 resolutions with respect to the matter were moved. I believe that every hon. gentleman who heard these discussions was convinced, that morally and equitably, Prince Edward Island was entitled to have her original representation restored. If a wrong has been done Prince Edward ' Island, this is the time and the place to right it, and I trust the committee, which will be appointed under this Bill, will have power to consider the claims of the province and to make a recommendation in accordance with them. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said that the committee could not deal with this matter, but I take it that this House can delegate to its committee any powers it wishes to. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition, thi3 afternoon, pointed out, that at one time it was proposed that the redistribution of constituencies should be submitted to a committee of judges, and consequently the right hon. gentleman evidently believes that under the British North America Act Parliament could delegate that power to the judges. If that be so, why cannot Parliament delegate equal authority to one of its own committees. Section 51 of the British North America Act provides:
On the completion of the census In the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and on each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such a manner, and from such time, as the Parliament of Canada from time to time provides.
This Parliament can, therefore, readjust, by such authority and in such manner as it may deem fit; and consequently this Parliament can lay down rules for the guidance

of its committee. That committee can make recommendation that Prince Edward Island is equitably and honestly entitled to six members in this House, and that recommendation could be inserted in the Bill. I have no doubt that the Imperial Parliament would, on the petition of this Parliament, if that were necessary, amend the British North America Act so as to give proper effect to the terms, in this respect, on which Prince Edward Island entered Confederation. As this matter will be discussed again during the session, I shall have something further to say on it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I have so many times spoken on this question in previous parliaments and in this, that I feel embarrassed in having again to address the House. I agree very sincerely with the suggestion of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition that the Prime Minister should withdraw the suggestion of referring the representation of Prince Edward Island to the committee. It is not with pleasure that I, or any other of the Maritime province members, look upon the reduction in the representation of our provinces, in view especially of the immense preponderance of representation that is bound to come from the West. At the same time I for one have always taken the ground that in this country we must adhere to the fundamental principles of the British North America Act. Whenever we undertake to deviate from those principles, we are always in danger of making our position worse than before.
While I agree with my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in standing firm by the principles of representation as outlined in our constitution, even for my sister province of Prince Edward Island, I do so because I believe that this Parliament has no power, as has been so clearly put by my right hon. friend- the leader of the Opposition, to deal with this question, and the committee therefore that would be appointed by this House has still less power to deal with this question. If we have no power in our hands, we cannot convey any power to the committee in respect to the matter. I believe that my right hon. friend the leader of the Government in making that suggestion has been carried away by sympathy for the Maritime provinces, more particularly for the smallest of the Maritime provinces. I wish to commend to him the words of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition to-day, that he will consider again and withdraw this recommendation which may perhaps only be useful in maintaining an agitation for representation

to which we have no right, and which can be given to us only by change of the constitution, and this Parliament has no power to change the constitution except by reference to the provinces and that cannot be done to-day.
We had a convention of the provincial premiers in October last, and the question was submitted to them. No understanding has so far been arrived at. They decided to leave the matter where it was, and therefore we should do the same until a new convention is held and then, perhaps, they may arrive at a unanimous decision. It would only be then that we could apply to the Parliament of Great Britain for a change of constitution. This cannot be done now and the country cannot wait until we have a change of constitution.
For my friends from Prince Edward Island I have the greatest possible sympathy. I am in the same position as they are, but perhaps I might be of some use to them in giving them the advice which I have given them in the past, that between the Maritime provinces, in order to strengthen our position in this Parliament, we have other means at our command. Therefore, we should direct our energies to those means that are practical and possible. We should unite the three Maritime provinces, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia into one province. This matter has already been brought up. It was brought up before Confederation, as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows very well, and Confederation was helped along by the idea of bringing the Maritime provinces together into one province. We would then be represented in this House by as large a number of members as any of the other provinces of the West are today. Possibly under the sympathetic views of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, we could give Prince Edward Island the four representatives which her people would like to keep to-day, because in the united province we could distribute our representation so as to give that island the representation which the people would like to keep while maintaining our dignity as well. My hon. friends from the Maritime provinces would willingly go into such a question again. I would suggest that we try to bring into Confederation Newfoundland with whom we have the same interest in every respect. Then our representation would be increased by say ten or twelve more, and we would be as strong a province as regards representation as any province in the Dominion.
As to what has been said about representation, it is very well known that the fathers of Confederation from the Maritime provinces would never have consented to representation by population unless the Senate had been constituted as a compensation for the representation in the House of Commons, and unless that representation had been made permanent and effective and proportionate. Therefore, the constitution of the Senate, in so far as it is made to represent the smaller bodies of Confederation, to represent the smaller provinces as well as the smaller bodies in every province concerned has not been made on the principle of the American Senate or of a similar body in any other country. It was made to meet the circumstances of Canada as a whole, as it was to be with that growing preponderance from the West. This Senate, therefore, has one chief object in view, that is, the protection of minorities. When I speak of minorities, I mean smaller provinces as well as minorities in the different provinces. Therefore, we cannot say tnat tnere is an incongruity in the fact that, after this redistribution of seats in the House, perhaps the province of Prince Edward Island will have as large a representation	in the Senate	as it has	in	theHouse of	Commons. If	the people	of	theMaritime	provinces do	not exert	themselves more than they	have done	in	the
past to keep their population at home, the time may come when New Brunswick and Nova Scotia may be represented in this House by fewer representatives than in the Senate, where for each of these provinces we have ten. In my opinion, the fathers of Confederation, knowing that this great development was bound to continue for centuries to come, were well aware that nothing would induce the people of the Maritime provinces to stand here only on representation by population. If we were to commence again to-day, I for one would not consent to see New Brunswick or the other Maritime provinces come into this Confederation under the principle of representation by population if we did not have some other means of security for the future.
It is said that the province of Prince Edward Island is under peculiar circumstances; and that when she came into Confederation, after having refused to do so for a certain number of years, she came in under the expectation that she was to be represented by six members in the House of Commons in perpetuity, and that the

representation would not be decreased no matter what her population might be in proportion to the population of the other provinces. On this point I entertain a different view. It may seem strange that the representatives from Prince Edward Island, after having opposed Confederation for a certain number of years, came in under the terms of the British North America Act; but I claim that if they did come in that Act, they came into Confederation conscientiously, and that the Government of that day that brought Prince Edward Island into Confederation did it conscientiously also. In the debates of the first days of Confederation much more will be found to justify my position than to justify the position taken by my hon. friend (Mr. McLean). The reason why the Government of that day did not feel justified in bringing Prince Edward Island into Confederation, except under the terms of the British North America Act, was that the same Government had committed the	error-perhaps	in good	faithof bringing British Columbia into Confederation in 1871 with .six members, though its population did not justify so large a representation, and of giving it a right to retain that number of members for all time to come. That was discussed in Parliament at the time, and I can say that it was because the Government of that day saw that they had made an error that they were determined not to repeat that error when Prince Edward Island came in. For authority I give you the very gentleman who in New Brunswick had been the strongest opponent of Confederation, particularly on this very point sf representation. I speak of the gentleman who was the first representative in this House of the county which I now have the honour to represent, Hon. T. W. Anglin, who for four years enjoyed the dignity which is now yours, Mr. Speaker, as President of this Chamber, and whose son now adorns the highest tribunal of this country. He was one of the great factors in the discussion which resulted in the decision of New Brunswick in favour of Confederation, and it was this very question of representation which caused him to oppose Confederation. He wielded a powerful influence, having a great newspaper at his command, the Freeman of St. John, and was besides a recognized authority on these questions. But, while he opposed Confederation, yet, when the final decision was reached, he was willing

to stand by the terms of the constitution. But for that very reason he was determined to see to it that it was maintained for British Columbia as well as for the Maritime provinces.
