maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you left the Chair at six o'clock, I was commencing to endeavour to demonstrate to this House, in reply to the hon. member for Prince Edward Island who had just taken his seat, that the Parliament of Canada, in 1871, committed an error in respect to the constitution when British Columbia was admitted into this Confederation with a representation of six members, which was not to be decreased, but was to be increased according to the terms of Confederation. The wording perhaps did not strike the attention of many members of Parliament or other people in Canada, but it was an infringement on the principle of representation by population, and if it was allowed to pass, no doubt it was with the expectation, justified in the hopes of every man in Canada, that the province of Nova Scotia, with her immense territory and her immense resources of every nature, would certainly be able to keep her representation in comparison with the other provinces. Meanwhile let me say to my friend from Prince Edward Island that, in my opinion, and in the opinion of any member of high authority in this country at the time and ever since, those six repre-

sentatives of the province of British Columbia, while they were talcing their seats in this House until that province acquired a sufficient population to allow it six seats in this House, were taking their seats unconstitutionally, and had virtually no moral right to be in this House. If I had had time to make some researches, 1 am sure I could quote eminent constitutional authorities to sustain this statement. Meanwhile I sympathize with my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island, who finds it hard that that province, coming into Confederation after British Columbia with the expectation in the minds of the people that their representation of six would not be diminished in the future, must submit to a reduction of representation. The terms of the Act bringing Prince Edward Island into Confederation leave no doubt as to the intent and spirit of the constitution itself when it reads that Prince Edward Island, having increased her population to such a number, should be admitted to Conferdation with a representation ot six members bur to be. readjusted according to the terms of Confederation. If the word ' readjusted ' had been used in the statute of British Columbia instead of the words ' to be increased according to the terms of the British North America Act, there would not have been any difficulty as to British Columbia. It is no doubt owing to the debate which took place in this Parliament on the bringing of British Columbia into Confederation that the Government in 1872 was more particular in not repeating the same error they had made in the case of British Columbia, and then, too, the principle of representation had been sustained by the representatives of the Maritime provinces, those who were here, ready, as I am to-day, to submit to the circumstances into which our constitution may bring us, with more or less representation in the future. I quoted my predecessor in *office, the Hon. Timothy Warren Anglin, who represented for fourteen or fifteen years the county which I now represent. I may also quote the name of Sir Albert Smith, who was a strong opponent of Confederation, but who strongly supported, the terms of Confederation after the provinces had been admitted, and who, although from the Maritime provinces, took the stand that I take to-day, that if we want to perpetuate the good will of the people of the different provinces and to work for their future happiness and for ours, we must stand by the principle of representation by population, 55
even if it involves a sacrifice on the part of some sections of the country. In a country like ours, with a territory stretching from ocean to ocean, with a population which is increasing by a million every year, so that in a few years we will have fifteen millions to twenty millions of people, we cannot expect that everybody will be equally satisfied, owing to the great diversity of interests that must exist in different sections of the country. For the sake of the future happiness of this country, we of the Maritime provinces are prepared to make sacrifices.
It is not merely the number of representatives that makes for the happiness of this country, but the good will of all. When I stand here to-day, begging, as I might say, not only my colleagues from the Maritime provinces, but the people at large, to stand by the terms of Confederation, I am consistent. That is the stand I have always taken. My first public act almost was to stand by the terms of Confederation under the most difficult circumstances. In 1873. by a iudsment of the Privy Council, the Catholic minority in the province of New Brunswick were told that we had no constitutional rights as to separate education. Young as I was, I was one of the first of the Catholic minority in the province of New Brunswick to stand by that judgment and to appeal to my people to stand by it, and direct our energies through other channels for the redress of our grievances. I took the same stand not very long ago, when the question came up of increasing the provincial subsidies. If my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition were here, I would recall to his memory that at that time I wrote him a letter telling him that I would be only too glad to see more money given to the provinces for the construction of roads and for educational purposes; but I pointed out that the money would have to be distributed according to population, and under the sole control of the provinces. I had a satisfactory reply from my leader, telling me that he held the same views, and he asked what I thought of a conference of all the provincial premiers. I replied mat I was perfectly agreeable to such a conference, and that I would adhere to whatever conclusion they reached; and to-day I take the same .stand.
Let me tell my right hon. friend that I am not alone in the province of New Brunswick in holding these views. Men ..who have devoted many years to .the



study of conditions in this country, men of high attainments and independent of politics, hold the same views, and I would be derelict in my duty if I did not take this oportunity of expressing my views and of begging the Prime Minister to withdraw, for the sake of Prince Edward Island, the suggestion he made to the committee. I fear that its effect would be to stir up a useless agitation. I, for one, hope that the members of this House will always be animated by a spirit of justice. I expect that every member who may come in from the far West will, when he enters this sanctuary of the Canadian people, be animated by a sense of justice and chivalry for the poor and weak. No Canadian wants charity, we want justice. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, in the words of the late D'arcy McGee, who compared Canada to a tree, carrying in its growth the true spirit of British institutions. It has already expanded and covered Canada from coast to coast, and in the course of a few years it will extend over the shores of Newfoundland. To repeat his own words, ' And of that tree every Canadian is always sure to get his fair share of the shelter and the shade.' With that hope, I call upon my right hon. friend to withdraw his suggestion to the committee. I thank you for your kind attention.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I have only a few words to say in speaking in reply on this Bill. My right hon. friend, in the course of his observations, did not take any pronounced exception to the principles which I had submitted for consideration in introducing the Bill. He went somewhat at length into the question of the extent to which county boundaries had been departed from in the readjustment of 1903. It is neither necessary nor desirable that I should go into that question at length to-night, because it will be a proper matter for the consideration of the committee. The right hon. gentleman dealt only with the province of Quebec. If he had taken the province of Ontario and some other provinces, he might have found a good many illustrations in addition to those with which he has favoured the House. In the province of Ontario I recall that the municipal boundaries were departed from in the case of the county of Carleton, the city of Ottawa, the county of Russell, the county of Fron-tenac, the city of Kingston, and I think also in the case of the county of Leeds; and in addition to that in relation to the territorial district of Nipissing. In the

province of Nova Scotia the county of Cape Breton was divided and a part of it added to the adjoining county of Victoria. In saying this, I do not at all intend to suggest that great consideration should not be given to the question of county boundaries. I only desire to repeat that, in connection therewith, another principle must be taken into account-the equalizing, to as reasonable an extent as possible, of the population within the various electoral districts which are to be established in Canada.
The right hon. gentleman was more or less exercised because I had left a blank in the Bill with respect to the representation of Prince Edward Island. But, in discussing that question, he did not even allude to the matters which I thought worthy of consideration by the House and by the committee, namely, the fact that the province of Prince Edward Island has alleged, and still alleges, whether rightly or wrongly, that there was an unfortunate mistake made in drawing up the terms of Confederation in that regard. Nor did he allude to what I thought was proper for the consideration of the House and the committee-the question as to whether or not it is a desirable thing that any province in Canada should have a smaller representation in the lower House than in the Senate. Nor did he pay any attention whatever to the suggestion which I made, that the population of Prince Edward Island, being almost entirely a rural population, it would be entitled, if situated in any other province in Canada, to have a representation of at least four members. Both he and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) seemed to be more or less disturbed about some proposed attempt to depart from the compact by which the various provinces were given representation upon a certain basis. My hon. friend from Pictou, as well as the right hon. gentleman himself, sought to enlighten me as to the capacity of this Parliament to deal with the question under consideration. I am not disposed at the present moment to debate the legal question, but it might be worth while, in passing, to allude to the fact that upon a strict application of the 51st section of the British North America Act in 1882, the province of Prince Edward Island would then have had its representation reduced to five members.
I did allude to the consideration put forward by my hon. friend from Kings, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes), but I alluded to it as a consideration present

to the minds of those who framed and introduced that Bill, and not as a legal ground which would have justified them in concluding that upon strictly legal considerations the province could have retained its membership. Given in the first place the unit fixed by the population of the province of Quebec and applying that unit to Prince Edward Island, you would thus find that the representation of that province must be reduced. Then when you came to seek relief from that result by reason of the provision of the 4th subsection of the 51st section of the British North America Act, the reason suggested by the hon. member of Kings would not justify a departure from the result arising from the first part of the section. If the conditions demanded by the provisions of that subsection were not capable of being invoked, the subsection could have no operation. However, that is by the way. I did suggest, in regard to Prince Edward Island, that at least that province ought to have the right to be heard, and I venture to propose that the province shall have the right to be heard before that committee, notwithstanding the apprehensions which have been expressed with very great eloquence and earnestness by the hon. member for Gloucester, New Brunswick (Mr. Turgeon). I am afraid that my hon. friend is of too timorous a frame of mind altogether, because no one is disposed to rush into an attempt to depart from the compact which was entered into at the time Prince Edward Island was brought into Confederation. The questions which have been presented for our consideration speak for themselves.
If my right hon. friend, who leads the Opposition, is somewhat exercised about my own attitude in this regard, I would like to tell him, if he were present, that if there has been any departure from the compact made between the original provinces in 1867, when a certain basis of representation in this Parliament was fixed, it seems to me that my right hon. friend is the only one who is to be credited with such a departure. When we, two years ago, in pursuance of a resolution passed by this House some years before, added a very large territory to the province of Quebec, we made two provisions which were fair, on the one hand, to the province of Quebec and, on the other hand, to the Maritime provinces and all the other provinces of Canada. We provided, by the terms of the Bill which at that time was 55J
passed by Parliament, that if there should be in the additional territory a population entitled to representation in this House of Commons it should receive that representation. That was fair to the province of Quebec. We also provided that, for the purpose of fixing the unit which should determine the representation of the Maritime provinces and the other provinces of Canada, the population within that added territory should not be taken into consideration. That was fair, as I say, on the one hand, for the province of Quebec, and it was absolutely fair, on the other hand, to the people of the Maritime provinces and the other provinces of Canada.
When my right hon. friend added 250,000 square miles to the province of Quebec in 1897 he took no such course as that. He enlarged the geographical unit upon which depends the representation of all the other provinces of Canada by about 250,000 square miles, and if there should be one person for every four square miles of territory inhabiting that added territory, the result would be that the unit which determines the representation, and will determine the representation of the Maritime provinces and of the province of Ontario for all time to come, would be increased by no less than one thousand. Every hon. gentleman in this House will understand that that would make a very material change, and would, I believe, if it were acted upon at the present time, change the representation of more than one province in Canada in the measure which we now propose. Therefore, in view of the fact that my right lion, friend has expressed so keen an anxiety that we depart in no measure whatever from the compact which was entered into at the time of Confederation, it would have been well for him at the time he made that change in 1897, to have had regard to the same considerations which affect him so deeply to-day.
My hon. friend from the county of Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has alluded to the methods by which the British North America Act has been changed in the past, or may be changed in the future, namely, by an address to His Majesty's Government asking that a certain change should be made in the Constitutional Act which is the charter of the people of this Dominion. That is one method; but perhaps my hon. friend from Pictou is not aware that other methods have also been established on more than one occasion since 1867, and that there have been occasions when legislation has been passed by

this Parliament admittedly, or probably, beyond the jurisdiction of this Parliament, accompanied with a stipulation that it should not be put into force until after an Act had been passed by the Imperial Parliament confirming the provisions which were therein set forth.
My hon. friend from Pictou also made certain observations with regard to the principles which should govern the committee. I would like to say, in so far as these are concerned, that while some of the principles which he laid down would be entirely desirable if they were practicable, I do not for a moment think that they would be practicable as determining the conclusions of the committee; nor are they	in force to-day in half
of	the	constituencies in Canada.
When the hon. gentleman expressed not only the importance but the necessity of having all the people within a constituency in direct relation with each other m a business way and otherwise, he certainly must have known that no such desirable result is possible. In my own county it is not possible; in his county I do not think it is possible; and there are many other constituencies in Canada in which such a result could not be obtained. At the same time, in so far as it can be obtained, I find no fault with the suggestion of my hon. friend.
In regard to certain observations addressed to me by my hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. J. J. Hughes) and in connection with which I am the innocent cause of that hon. gentleman thinking it necessary to read to the House the whole of a very excellent speech which he delivered in 1903-1 beg to say to him that it is not by any means my desire to misrepresent him, and I am perfectly willing to leave his speech and my observations to the judgment of the members of the House. The hon. gentleman may have one opinion in regard to his observations and I may have another, but I can assure him that my opinion is as sincerely held by me as his opinion can possibly be held by him. I do not know of one argument that has ever been raised against the claims of Prince Edward Island which was not embodied in the speech of my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) in 1903. If he is able to state now one single argument ever put forward against the claims of his province which he did not put forward in that speech, I will yield the floor to him and let him state what it is. That his province was debarred by reason of

acquiescence, he emphasized over and over again.

speechtext: Did I make one statement that was not correct, according to the British North America Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I stated that my hon.
friend had argued against the contention of Mr. Hackett, and I said he had argued strongly against it. The hon. gentleman himself will not deny that he argued against the contention of Mr. Hackett, and if I do him the compliment to say he argued strongly, surely he ought not to find fault with me.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the right hon. gentleman say that I made one statement contrary to the proper interpretation of the British North America Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend did not
confine himself to the British North America Act; he put forward the theory of acquiescence. He said Prince Edward Island could not make any claim now because of acquiescence, and in the concluding part of his speech he said that Prince Edward Island could not raise its claim now because of the lapse of time. Further, he put aside the contention which had been raised then, and is still raised, that there had been an actual mistake as between the two contracting parties in 1873, and he declared that the resultant condition was due simply to the fact that the gentlemen who represented Prince Edward Island on that occasion were guilty of an oversight. He did not contend that there had been a mistake, but that there had been neglect and forgetfulness. Under the circumstances, I do not know how I could have criticised the observations of my hon. friend, if I alluded to them at all, except as I have done. My hon. friend certainly argued against Mr. Hackett; he will not deny that, and I thought he argued strongly against Mr. Hackett; but if he desires me to withdraw that, and to say that he tried to argue strongly but argued weakly, I will let the matter go at that.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has referred to the number of the committee, and has made an appeal to us to increase the number from seven to nine. Hon. gentlemen on the opposite side were content, and we were content in 1903, to have a committee of only seven. The argument is put forward that inasmuch as there are nine provinces now, the committee should consist of nine, there having been only seven provinces in 1903

and seven members on the committee. Perhaps hon. members who have not looked at the record will be a little surprised to learn that although there were seven provinces in 1903, only three of those seven provinces were represented on that committee. Ontario had three members: Mr. Sutherland, Mr. Hyman and Mr. Haggart; Quebec had two members: Mr. Fitzpatrick and Mr. Monk; the Maritime provinces had one member: myself; and the Northwest Territories had one member: Mr. Davis. The provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, were not represented at all on that committee. If we are going to have every province in Oanada represented on both sides it would involve a committee of 18 or 20 members, and I do not suppose anything like that is suggested.
I am disposed to give the subject every consideration, although I think my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will agree with me on reflection that for the purposes of a conference, as it is called, of this character, the smaller the number of the committee, within reasonable limits, the better. That is my idea, and for that reason I acquiesced in the proposal of the right hon. gentleman in 1903. Still, when such a suggestion is made by our friends on the other side, it ought not to be lightly dismissed, and for that reason I will not give a definite reply to-night, but at the conclusion of my observations I will move the adjournment of the debate in order that I may on Thursday or Friday next- in the meantime having conferred with my right hon. friend and possibly some other gentlemen on the other side of the House- be able to say whether a committee of seven members or nine members is really most likely to be the more effective. It is my desire, as far as may be reasonably possible to meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen opposite in this matter. What I have said is only with the view of pointing out that there was no attempt in 1903 to represent the various provinces of Canada on that committee. The only object which governed the constitution of the committee in 1903, was to have four members from one side of the House and three members from the other side, who would be able, conferring with each other, to present views which would represent the opinions of the two sides of the House in regard to matters of a possibly controversial character, and to endeavour, by reasonable compromise, to
reach an agreement, if possible. If that was the object in 1903, I cannot at the moment see the advantage of increasing the committee from seven to nine members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I
do not think the increase in membership is suggested with the idea of having a member from each province, from each side of the House, which would be absurd; but does not the right hon. gentleman see that in our general rough division of the country we have the Maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, and the West, and the idea in the minds of some of us was that if local knowledge were required as to the various districts, it would be a little invidious to make a distinction against the West as between the other geographical divisions of the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I realize the point of view of my hon. friend from Red Deer, and any observation of his is always entitled to careful consideration. I would like to point out to him that the only two provinces established in the West at that time, Manitoba and British Columbia, had no representation upon the committee. So far as our side of the committee was concerned, we had absolutely no representation upon it in respect of either British Columbia, Manitoba or the Territories. As a matter of fact, the constitution of the committee in 1903 was rather curious, as it turned out in the end. Mr. Monk and Mr. Haggart, who were associated with me on the committee, were not perhaps as attentive upon it as I was myself, for the reason that Mr. Haggart did not desire very much to deal with details apd Mr. Monk confined his attention almost entirely to the province of Quebec, which was arranged between himself and Mr. Fitzpatrick without any great difficulty, as I understand. The result was that, outside of the province of Quebec, I had imposed upon my feeble shoulders the burden of every province in Canada so far as the Opposition was concerned.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I hope my right hon. friend is not vindictive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Not at all. I cannot say that I enjoyed the task very much, because the session lasted for seven months and thirteen days. We did not get away that year until the 24th of October. I found it necessary also to give a good deal of attention to a very important measure which was introduced that year, known as a Bill to establish a National Transcontinental railway. Between the Redistribution Bill

and the Bill to establish a National Transcontinental railway, I am free to say that the session of 1903 made upon me a profound impression which I do not think will ever be obliterated.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to make a suggestion. Does my right hon. friend appreciate the difference between this year and 1903, in respect to the number of constituencies in v estern Canada that will have to be dealt with now and that did not require to be dealt with in 1903? I simply present this suggestion a-s something that may have weight with my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I appreciate the difference 'between 1903 and the present year, not only in that respect but otherwise, and I will give to this suggestion of my hon. friend the best consideration that I can.
I have nothing further to add except to say that, when my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) makes those remarkable calculations with rega d to the majority which is represented by a certain number of persons in Parliament today, every hon. member knows that calculations of that kind do not amount to much and that one could make an endless variety of such remarkable calculations by taking up a certain number of constituencies in one or other of the provinces of Canada. As a matter of fact, in 1908, my hon. friends on the other side of the House, although 1 aving a maiority of something over forty in this House, had a minority, if I am not mistaken, of the popular vote. That does not really amount to very much in our system of popular government because, where the majorities on one side are very large and on the other side happen in many cases to be narrow, the result which I 'have just indicated may be very easily brought about, and no way of avoiding it can be reached unless we adopt the proposal of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), that we should enter into one of those elaborate schemes for proportionate representation.
I remember having given some consideration to that subject some years ago. It was very strongly advocated by Earl Grey when he was Governor General of Canada, and I think he still continues to advocate it. But I am bound to say that under the system of party government, it seems to me-as I told Earl Grey at the time, although I was then in Opposition-to involve very considerable difficulties, because, if you had exactly the same proportion of representation in Parliament as would be determined
r.Mr. Borden.]
by popular vote, you never could have a working majority in the House of Commons. Previously to 1908, my hon. friends on the other side of the House, as I calculate, would have had, according to the popular vote, a majority of only three and a half in this Parliament.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And one middle bencher.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
One middle bencher;
and every one of us knows that it is necessary and desirable, whether one party or the other be in power, that a reasonable working majority should be on hand. I do not very well see how we could carry on our system of party government without that. I do not intend, however, to discuss the subject at length. It is sufficient to say that we are prepared to give it consideration, but I do not think we shall attempt to put it into force at this readjustment. Perhaps in the course of the next decennial census we may have further light on the subject. Further con-isideration in the meantime might bring about changes of opinion.

You had better not
give any assurance as to the future.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

No. I will leave the
number of representatives on the committee in abeyance for the present. I move that the debate be now adjourned.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In the apparent determination of my right hon. friend to submit the question of Prince Edward Island to the committee, and in the event of the committee allowing the four representatives to the province of Prince Edward Island and thereby reversing the decision of the Privy Council, which has pronounced upon the matter, would my right hon. friend be at once ready and willing to give the four representatives to the province of Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend has mistaken me. I am not submitting any decision of the Privy Council to the committee, and, with respect to what I shall do, I will remind my hon. friend from Gloucester that I have just been cautioned by my hon. friend from Westmorland not to make any promises as to the future.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What day will the committee be named?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will propose to resume the adjourned debate on Thursday, and then the committee will be immediately constituted. In the meantime I

will take the opportunity of conferring on the matter with the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition.
Motion of Mr. Borden agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Foster for Committee of Supply:

I would like to discuss
for a few moments the questions which I placed on the Order Paper the other day and the answers given to the same.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are these questions answered and disposed of? If this is an anticipating of questions on the Order Paper, it would not be permissible to discuss them now.
They were answered, and it is the answers I wish to deal with.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If this were held to be referring to a past debate, of course, it would not be in order; otherwise it would be permissible. The rule is that answers given by ministers of the Crown are given in the exercise of their best judgment and must be accepted as given.

The answers are perfectly plain, but I wish to make some comment on them. The questions and their answers are as follows:
1.	What stone was specified to be used in the Brantford public building by the architect?
2.	Was it to be Canadian?
3.	What was the estimated value?
4.	From whom was it purchased?
5.	From where was it purchased?
6.	Who was the contractor for cutting the stone?
7.	Where was his home when contract was made ?
Mr. Rogers:
1.	Georgetown, Ontario, was specified.
2.	Yes.
3.	No detailed estimate was made for the stone.
4.	The stone used was Berea, Ohio, sandstone, as the price quoted by the contractor in his tender was considerably lower than the price for Georgetown stone and this tender was accepted.
5.	Berea, Ohio.
6 and 7. The cutting of the stone was included in the contract awarded to P. H. Secord and Sons, Limited, Brantford.
One would almost wonder if all the loudmouthed protestations of loyalty to imperial trade and of desire to patronize home manufactures on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite were merely for the purpose of
deceiving the people. In the last election, from end to end of this country, there were protestations by our friends on the other side that we should trade within the empire and should patronize home manufactures. This referred even to the conduct of private individuals in the carrying on of their business. But here we find the Government itself declaring in the first place by their specifications for a public building that Canadian stones should be used, and then going outside and buying-from whom? From the Yankees, the very people to whom we were going to be annexed to if private individuals bought from them, the very people to whom we were going to be made an adjunct if we even trade with them. It seems almost impossible to believe that our friends opposite should stoop so low as they proclaim it, as to buy from people like the Yankees. And, above all, where do you suppose this building was constructed? Why, in the riding of my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), the lord high chancellor of the doctrine of patronage of home manufactures. And at that the earthquake did not come until the other day.

He is the evangel of
imperialism.

Why, he is the John the Baptist of the movement. But that is not the worst of it. I understand from a very reliable person who visited the works that the foreman employed on the stone-cutting -and employed in contravention of the alien labour law-was a Yankee, and that some of the other men employed on the work were Yankees. In Brantford! Think of it!
Now, that is the farcial side of the question, but there is a serious side. The answer to question No. 4 says that the stone used was Berea, Ohio, sandstone, as the price quoted by the contractor in his tender was considerably lower than the price for Georgetown stone, and this tender was accepted. Mr. Speaker, there is a rule of commerce throughout Canada, an absolute rule, that when tenders are called for on specifications, and the specifications are afterwards changed, every man who has tendered is allowed to amend his tender or new tenders are asked for under the new specifications. In this particular instance, the stone specified was Georgetown, Ontario, which was dearer. Now, some of the tenderers complained that somebody had the inside tracks with this Government, and that somebody must have been

the lowest tenderer, considering that he was allowed to use Ohio stone in place of Georgetown stone. The first aspect of the question to which I referred may be merely an illustration to the Canadian public that the loud protest of hon. gentlemen opposite were merely for the purpose, if I may say so, of deceiving the public. But this is a serious question. In private life no honourable individual or corporation would permit the changing of specifications for one tenderer without giving every tenderer the same opportunity. And as to the cutting of the stone, surely there could be found in Canada a foreman capable of overseeing this work. Has it come to this, that we Canadians not only cannot build battleships, but we cannot cut stone ?	1
merely give these answers to the House as they were given to me. I asked the questions purely to get at the truth of the rumour in our section of the country that these facts as they have been given by the department were the real facts in this case.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) himself admitted that he tried to be farcial, and I am sure that in that respect, if in no other, he succeeded in his remarks. But he has said that there is a serious side to this question which he has brought before the House, and it is on that serious side that I propose to say a word or two. He make the statement that somebody must have the inside track with the Government and that this accounts for the condition of which he complains. As far as I know, no man has an inside track in the letting of contracts in connection with the Public Works Department of Canada. In respect to the contract as let for the building of a post office in the city of Brantford, I have to say that it was let upon the merits of the tenders as put in according to the terms of the specifications and conditions under which the tenders were to be received. The facts are that we had, I think, two or three tenders for that work. Secord & Company tendered, according to specifications with the use of Georgetown stone, for $273,108; and with the use of New Brunswick stone for $259,980. The Schultz Bros. Company, Limited, tendered, according to the specifications with the use of Georgetown stone, for $273,908; and with the use of New Brunswick stone, for $247,718. The specifications were followed absolutely and correctly. The specifi-
.
cations contained the following clause in respect to stone:	[DOT]
The facing stone (excepting granite) on elevations from top to base course to top of coping, tower, pent house, sills to all windows, lintels to all windows and doors, copings, band courses and where coloured umber to be approved Logan stone from Georgetown, Ont., or other approved stone of equal quality, to the entire satisfaction of the chief architect.
We have here the facts of the case. When the tenders were received it is true that Secord and Company tendered for $244,000 under the suggestion of using American Berean sandstone, a stone which has been used to a very large extent in the Dominion of Canada. It is the stone of which the post office and the Bank of Montreal in the city of Ottawa are built. When it became a question of whether we should accept the tenders of the Georgetown stone or of the Berean stone I at once said to the Deputy Minister of my department that we must, if we possibly could, use Canadian stone. But, on a consideration of the question, it was shown that there was a difference of $28,000 in the cost of this stone. The chief architect, who was to be the judge of the matter, was appealed to and stated that in his opinion the Berean stone was fully as good as, if not better than the Georgetown stone. That was the simple and the only reason why the tender was accepted for Berean stone for the construction of the building in the city of Brantford in preference to the stone first specified, known as Georgetown stone.
This is simply a recital of the facts in order that the hon. member for North Oxford may not be carried away with any misunderstanding of the true conditions of the letting of the contract and of the tender which has been referred to in respect of the construction of the post office in Brantford.
I say that the contract was let in accordance with the recommendation of the chief architect of the Department of Public Works. The chief architect of that department is a man known, I think, to every hon. member of this House; and I am sure that no hon. member would say that I would be justified in paying $28,000 more for Georgetown stone when the chief archi- , tect said that the Berean sandstone was really a better stone than the Georgetown stone and could be secured at a cost of $28,000 less to the people of Canada.

I quite agree with the Minister of Public Works that in letting contracts, either in that department or in the Department of Rail-

87a
ways and Canals, so far as my experience has gone, and I have had some considerable experience, there is no one who has inside information; and I quite appreciate his other statement, that the chief architect of the Department of Public Works is one of the best men we have in the public service in Canada. I have known him for a good many years and I am not so much criticising the, position which the chief architect took in allowing American stone to be used in this contract as I am criticising this particular phase of it, that I do not think the Government should allow American stone to be used at all. I do not think the department should have specified Georgetown stone. We have in the Niagara district limestone quarries, the Queenston quarries and the Beamsville quarries and the Thorold quarries, which produce the finest stone that this or any other country can produce. It has been used to build and construct the heaviest work that has been constructed in Canada and. it can be procured at a cheaper figure, I believe, than the Georgetown stone can be procured, and just as cheap as the Ohio sandstone can be procured. The Government specified Georgetown stone and consequently the men who are interested in the, Queenston, Beamsville and Thorold quarries would not tender, although they might have been able to supply the stone at as low a figure as it was supplied by the contractor who got his supply from the United States. It is that phase of it that I desire particularly to criticise, namely that the Government should not specify any particular class of stone except as to it being a good quality of limestone such as would be approved of by the chief architect of the department, whether Georgetown, Beamsville or Queenston stone. And when we come to the point of stone-cutters, we have in Niagara district the best stone-cutters the world can produce. I would call that to the attention of the Minister of Public Works and of the Government generally, that if they want stone-cutters all they have to do is to come to the county of Welland and they can get the best stone-cutters the world can produce. Or they can come to the county of Lincoln. I see my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) smiling at that. He has stone-cutters in his constituency, and I am surprised that he has not made something of a disturbance in regard to this.

I would like to draw the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that this was a contract let to Secord & Sons. They had a perfect right to employ whom
they wished so long as they did not violate the Alien Labour Act.

It has been suggested
that the Government allow the Alien Labour Act to be broken so that these stone cutters could come in. But I wish to call the attention of the minister to this one fact which is within my own knowledge: it is absolutely impossible for a Canadian to go into the United States and to get such a contract as that; they would simply be barred out, and I think it is time we began to bar the people of the United States from coming over here and using American stone and American stonecutters on a Government building. We are just as capable of doing the work as the people of the United States. It may be said that this is political talk and for effect generally, but I do not wish it to be so considered. I believe that we in Canada are capable of doing our own work, and of doing it as efficiently and as cheaply as it can be done, and I, for one, am prepared to stand by the principle that we should keep Canada for the Canadians in that particular and use our own stone and our own stone cutters even if it costs a little more. I do not wish to insinuate that any contractor had any inside information or that he could possibly have got any inside information from the department.

I think I know a little about this question, and I would like to say to my hon. friend that he is barking up entirely the wrong tree in his attempt to fasten any wrong-doing on the Public Works Department in connection with the Brantford public building. If we had got one-quarter as good value from the contracts let by the Government my hon. friend has supported so-vigorously, he might have got up and criticised this question. He has shown a lamentable want of knowledge of the facts. The Minister of Public Works has made the facts plain. In the first place the specifications called for Georgetown stone or other of equal quality. What are the facts in regard to Georgetown stone? The minister has shown that the building would have cost $28,000 more, if it had been built of Georgetown stone instead of the stone . selected. Another point was, that the Georgetown quarries could not turn out enough stone for that building even if we got the whole output for two years.
Why was that stone specified if you could not get enough of it?

When the specifications weTe made out, it was not known that we could not get the Georgetown stone. We understood that there was a very large deposit of stone, and that there would be no trouble as to the quantity; but when the tenderer examined the quarry he found that he could not get enough stone to complete that building even if he used the whole output of his quarry in two years.

My hon. friend said that the specifications called for Georgetown stone or other of equal quality. I was only going by the answer I received from the department, which specified Georgetown stone and says nothing about 'other of equal quality'.
I am speaking by the book.
Which book?
The book is the specifications as written.
Then the answer is untrue.

I am giving what I know to be the facts. The specifications called for Georgetown stone, or other of equal quality. Then it was found that the Georgetown stone would cost $28,000 more. My endeavour was to have Canadian stone used in the building, but my hon. friend who has to account to the public for the expenditure of money was of the opinion that $28,000 was too much to pay for one building, as between Canadian * and American stone. There were three or four tenderers, and I may say to my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that the contract will stand thorough investigation as to its straightness. No insinuations which he has made are worthy of consideration. The lowest tenderer-a man who is doing an honest and good job-got the work. My hon. friend has made an endeavour to appeal to labour and has named the foreman. I am not in a position to give the nationality of the foreman stonecutter, but I can tell my hon. friend that ninety-five per cent of the stonecutters on that job are British subjects.
I did not say they were not.

My hon. friend just picks out one man on the building. Surely if these American come here to settle they have a right to work. I

visit the building almost every day and, as I said, my hon. friend can rest assured that 95 per cent of the stone-cutters on that building are Canadians and British subjects. Mr. Secord, the contractor, is doing the best work ever seen in the city of Brantford, and he is giving 100 cents on the dollar on that job. The whole matter from start to finish is being conducted in the most thorough manner. The site was purchased from the city of Brantford and the property is today worth more than double what was paid for it. I do not mean to say that Brantford intended to be over-liberal but they sold the property on which this building stands to the Government, so that the public might get the benefit, if there was any benefit in it. The building is being rapidly pushed to completion in a way that could not -have been done if we had chosen Canadian stone. I brought to the attention of the minister various Canadian stones, and it was found that every one of these would cost considerably more than the one chosen, and some of them would have to be transported some thousands of miles. It is a lamentable fact that within a distance of one hundred miles of Brantford you cannot find a first class stone in large quantities, and I say it with all deference to the constituency that has been mentioned by my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German). If he has a good kind of stone there I would like him to name one first class building in which it has been used. I do not know of one, and I have looked at several public buildings and endeavoured to come to a conclusion as to the best stone. I think the Government ought to be upheld because they have saved the country $28,000 by using this particular stone. The Chief Architect said that this stone was equal to the best, and therefore I think the criticism of my hon. friend from North Oxford is entirely aside from the question. The whole matter is just as honest and above board as any contract ever let by any Government, and if he has any doubt about that, I would be willing to have the most full investigation in regard to the whole matter.

It is rather
an interesting thing to see my hon. friend rushing to the defence of the proposition that you can get better stone in the United States to build Canadian buildings with than you can in Canada, and get it cheaper. If my hon. friend has attempted to prove anything in the remarks he has made, that

apparently was the object of his ambition. It means that when the Minister of Public Works came to ask for tenders for this work, he apparently was not aware of the fact that somewhere else in this country there was some stone other than the Georgetown quarry stone. All over the country there are quarries producing stone of a most admirable quality, such stone as the large banks and the great commercial buildings are being constructed of in different cities in Canada. Why did the Minister of Public Works confine the tenders for this particular building to a stone that he knew the quarry had run out of?
No, no.

Yes, because the
hon. member for Brantford says so.
I did not say so.
My hon. friend from Brantford did not say anything of the kind.

What did the hon.
member for Brantford say?

I will tell the hon.
gentleman.

I am dealing with
the Minister of Public Works. What did the hon. member for Brantford say?

The hon. member for
Brantford said that it was impossible to get the stone out as quickly as it would have been required for the construction of the building at Brantford.

Did the' Minister
of Public Works, or any of the officials of his department, know when they made that a condition of the contract, that they could not get Georgetown stone?
Apparently they did not.

Well, then, the result is that we have the fact established that the Minister of Public Works specified and prescribed as the one and only stone that could be placed in this building, a stone coming from a quarry in regard to which they had made no inquiries whatever to find out whether they could get any stone or not. The hon. member for Brantford tells us that this stone which was stipulated as the only stone which could be used came from a quarry where you could not get it inside of two years.

The hon. gentleman
does not want to misrepresent me.
No.
I did not say that. I said that the tenders called for Georgetown or some other stone of similar quality. Why does the hon. gentleman leave out the latter part of it?

For the very good
reason that the hon. member for Brantford is not the Minister of Public Works in this Government, and that if any member of. this House wants to get a statement as to what was prescribed and approved of for this work, he does not go to the hon. member for Brantford to find out, but he goes to the Minister of Public Works, who, in response to the question of my hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who wanted to know what stone vras specified, answered that stone of the Georgetown quarry was specified. What is the use of the hon. member for Brantford coming here and, in order to extricate himself and his friends from a difficulty, telling us that this statement of the Minister of Public Works is absolutely incorrect? Contractors were told:	You
can put no stone in that building but Georgetown stone. The Minister of Public Works has told us that the stone that he specified was the Georgetown stone, and when he found that this stone which had been specified came from a quarry could not produce any stone for two years, what did my hon. friend do? These gentlemen, who did not want any truck or trade with the Yankees, said:	You cannot get any
stone in Canada; Canadian stone is no good, except this stone that you cannot get out of the Georgetown quarries within two years; we will not bother looking up and down the country to find whether there is any stone to be got in Canada, but we will take Ohio sandstone; that is the best of all; it is better than any Canadian stone, and besides you can get it cheaper. We, on this side of the House, are all good enough Canadians to say to the Minister of Public Works: If you had used stone from any other Canadian quarry, even if it had cost a little more than Ohio sandstone, we would not have complained about it. We would give the minister some credit for realizing that Canada had some natural industries that deserve to be patronized. It was not necessary, especially in the case of a public building belonging to Canada, to blazen it abroad and to tell the men who are connected with the construction of public works in the country: If you want to erect a public building for the

Canadian Government, you must not buy Canadian stone for the purpose of doing it.
What about free food?

My hon. friend, the alarm clock, is starting again. However, it has been proved beyond the shadow of a doubt to the House and to the country that, in the estimation of this Government, Canadian stone is no good when you can get American stone to be used in public buildings.

I just desire to say that Georgetown is in the county I represent. I know the quarry referred to. The demand for Georgetown stone is certainly very great, and I am not surprised that this contractor could not get a sufficient quantity of stone in time to finish his contract from that quarry on account of the large demand for Georgetown stone. I will undertake to say that there is no better quality of free stone in the province of Ontario than is taken out of the Georgetown quarry.
It is better than American stone?

It may be far superior, but, unfortunately, Mr. Logan,, whose name is given as being the proprietor of the quarry, was not able to supply the stone in sufficient quantity at the time it was needed. That does not say one word against the quality of the stone; nor yet does it say one word against the quantity of the stone. There is a mountain of this stone right where the quarry is. If the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) wanted to erect a very large building within a reasonable distance of the quarry I have no doubt that an abundance of stone could be obtained provided sufficient time was given to take it out.
Why had you to go to the States to get it?

Well, now, the hon. gentleman had better be patient. I think he has had that fully explained to him. There was a limited time to get this stone. I never heard anything of this matter before, but it appears that the Georgetown quarry was not able to supply this stone in the quantity that was wanted and in the time provided for in the contract. There is no evidence that the Georgetown quarry could not have supplied the stone if a reasonable time had been given or if they had had sufficient notice. I see the hon. member for West Lamhton (Mr. Pardee) smil-

ing. The post office in his town is built from stone taken from the Georgetown quarry. The post office was built by the Government that he supported and I will undertake also to say that he does not find any fault with it and that he will not say that the stone taken from that quarry is not of the best.
We do not say that there is anything against the stone.

The hon. member for Pictou tried to give a black eye to this stone. The hon. gentleman does not know this quarry. It is being worked all the time full force and were it not for the terrible demand for Georgetown stone I have no doubt that this building at Brantford would have been built of Georgetown stone. The hon. gentleman must take all these circumstances into consideration. The Georgetown quarry is no one-horse affair. It is not limestone. It is the best quality of free stone. It is not like the limestone that they have in Welland county. It is a very fine quality of stone and as evidence of that let me say that a building was erected in my county during last year and the cut stone required for that building was taken out of the Georgetown quarry. It was approved by all parties and it also had my approval. It had the approval of everybody that looked at it. It was pronounced by everyone as a very superior quality of stone.
Why was it not put in the Brantford building?

How many times does my hon. friend want to know that ? I said that the men who are running this quarry, if they had sufficient notice, might have been able to supply the stone necessary; but owing to the tremendous demand for Georgetown stone, they could not get it out on time. The hon. gentleman had better take a run up to Georgetown and see the immense quantity of the superior stone that is being shipped from there, and then we will hear less complaints from him. I could not sit quietly in my seat and hear the hon. gentleman speak in that way of the quarry-
That you represent.

No, but in the
county I represent.
It was the member for Brantford, and not I, who reflected on the quality of the stone.

I listened to the hon. gentleman from Brantford, and I did

not hear him cast any reflection on the quality of the Georgetown stone. It has been said that the American stone has been obtained for less money, and I am not doubting that, because I do not know anything at all about the matter; but I do know that if Georgetown stone is not a better stone than the American stone, the demand for it would not be so great as it is. You must take into consideration the superior quality of the Georgetown stone when you remember the demand there is for it. I have no brief from Mr. Logan to praise the quality of this stone; I know it is a hard quarry to work, but I know they dig an immense quantity of stone out of it, and I do say it is stone of a very superior quality.
Hear, hear.

I do not think I am making any mistake when I say that the Georgetown stone is of superior quality, and it would have been just as well for the hon. member for Pictou if he did not cast any reflections on it.
What I said was, that it was better than the American stone.

The member for
Brantford has told us that 95 per cent of the men who work on that building are Canadians, and I have no doubt he is quite correct, as he usually is, in any statement he makes.	[DOT]
You mean he is as correct in that as in any statement he makes ?

No, I said he is as correct in that statement as he usually is in any statement he makes in this House. Hon. gentlemen opposite having cast reflections on the Georgetown stone, I trust they are now satisfied that it is stone of a very superior quality.

The hon. member for
Halton (Mr. Henderson) seems to be somewhat perturbed for fear we will not think the Georgetown stone is a stone of excellent quality, but he need not be alarmed on that score, because I can tell him that the Sarnia post office is built of Georgetown stone, and as he has invited hon. members to look at that stone in its natural state in the quarry, I invite them to come and see the finished product in the Sarnia post office. A remarkable fact about all this is, that it was well known, or it ought to have been well known when the specifications for the contract were prepared, that tlie stone could not have been obtained from Georgetown for two years. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) says the manager of the quarry told him that.
I never said anything of the kind.
Well, it was so understood then.
I do not know how it could have been understood.

The hon. member for
Brantford said the stone could not be obtained from Georgetown for two years.
I think it was the hon. member for Pictou who said that.
I never said anything of the kind.

Well, it was said, whoever said it, and it is not denied there is enough stone at Georgetown to supply the contract on the specification which called for that stone. But when the Government knew they could not possibly get the stone from the Georgetown quarry, there was nothing in the world to prevent them asking for tenders from some other Canadian quarry. Instead of that they rushed off to the United States to get the stone. No doubt they went to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), who was most anxious to have a public building in his constituency, and they said to him: we cannot get the Georgetown stone for two years, but we will get you stone from those terrible Yankees. And, you can imagine the hon. member horrified to think that the Yankees were to be traded with, but at the same time saying: if that is the case, I want to please my constituents, I want to be a good fellow, go ahead, never mind the other Canadian quarries, buy from the Yankees, it will do just as well. That is really the whole story. My hon. friend from Halton says there is a mountain of stone to be had at Georgetown, but it was not to be obtained for this Canadian public building. It is like the cry: water, water all around and not a drop to drink. . There was a mountain of stone there but the Government could not get it, and hence it was that, presuming the .Georgetown quarry could not supply the stone, instead of asking for new 'tenders, and giving other Canadian quarries a chance, this Government that two years ago was howling from the house tops: have nothing to do with

the Yankees, said: we will give no other Canadian industry a chance; we will give our wicked friends in Ohio the opportunity to supply this stone, and, anyway, we will get it cheaper there than in Canada. Well, I wonder how it would be with regard to ploughs. I do not think my hon. friend would for a moment stand for that. He would say: you can buy the stone from the Yankees, but keep your hands off me when it .comes to ploughs. The whole story is summed up in this: that the member for Brantford, finding he could not get Canadian stone to have the building erected speedily, went back on all the tenets he preached in September, 1911, and said: I will -swallow myself to this extent, and I will have just a little to do with the Yankees, if it helps me, the member for Brantford.

The discussion on this subject is a unique commentary on what transpired in this Parliament in 1903 and 1904, with respect to the Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. I remember how some hon. gentlemen opposite sat up nights trying to work some section into the Acts whereby the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the Transcontinental Commission would be prevented from using any foreign or American -material in the construction of that railway. There are to be found to-day clauses in these Bills which prohibit the use of material other than Canadian, where it is possible to secure it. We hear a different story to-night. The hon. gentleman from Halton seems to think there is only one stone quarry in Canada, and I take his word for it that the Georgetown stone is splendid stone and that there are mountains of it there, but I would remind him that there are other productive quarries in the Maritime provinces and elsewhere. He told us that the Georgetown quarry was not by any means a one-horse affair, but he succeeded in convincing the House that those who operate it are operating it as a one-horse affair, or eke they could have produced stone enough to build one public building in the city of Brantford. I think my hon. friend in that way deprecated the quarry in his constituency. Why did not my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works turn his eye towards the Maritime provinces? If he wants splendid quarries, he will find them there. He will find evidences of those quarries and samples of the stone from them in the municipal building in the city of Toronto; he will find sandstone from Nova Scotia and

New Brunswick, and from the county of Westmorland, in that splendid building in the city of Toronto and in other splendid buildings. I think the stone would be sufficiently good to be used even in a public building in the city of Brantford, represented by my hon. friend. But, no! they must go to Berea, and the justification of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is that private individuals have done so; that the banks, railway corporations and other corporations of the country in the construction of great buildings in our large cities have bought stone from Berea and other sections of the state of Ohio. True it is, but a party that fought night after night and complained because there might be a danger of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company purchasing material for the construction of its railway outside of Canada, a party that took up the time of this House complaining because of the employment of engineers who were American citizens in connection with the survey of the transcontinental line of railway, a party that took that attitude and then take the attitude that they are taking to-night, surely should be condemned and their attitude is its own condemnation.
On the motion of Mr. Foster for Committee of Supply:

I want to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to an Order of the House passed on the 20th of January, 1913, for the return of certain papers in connection with the officials of the Dorchester penitentiary, as to their appointments and promotions. It is not a very long return, but it has not yet been furnished. That is a grievance that I think I have a right to place before His Majesty before we resolve ourselves into Committee of Supply to furnish money for the purposes of government.
I want to call particular attention to the fact that certain information for which I have asked during this session, in fact at the beginning of this session, from the Department of Railways and Canals, has been withheld and is not forthcoming. It is very important for this House, in the consideration of certain questions, to have the full facts of what is known as the Gutelius-Bosworth agreement. It cannot be a very long document, and the papers in connection with it cannot be very voluminous. This document was promised by my right hon. friend the leader of the Government in October last to a deputation

which interviewed him from the city of St. John. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) promised his friends in the city of St. John that a copy of that agreement would be sent forward. They have not received it. This House ordered that we should have a copy, and it has not yet been brought down. I think that I have reason and hon. members have reason to complain of the very serious delays that are occurring with respect to information that is sought for from the Department of Railways and Canals. Questions that were on the Order Paper at the opening of the session have not been answered up to this moment, questions that are important, questions that do not require a lengthy answer. Perhaps the information may be in Moncton, but that is no excuse or justification. There is a private wire between the Department of Railways and Canals and the railway offices in the city of Moncton; the department are in communication almost hourly with those offices. This information surely should be given.
I take the fourth question on the Order Paper, which is as to whether or not a water supply has been furnished in connection with a certain station. Thirty minutes' work on the part of a clerk could prepare that information. The sixth question-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is not in order in taking up subjects on the Order Paper and discussing them. It is not permissible to anticipate a subject on the Order Paper and to discuss it.

I cannot discuss those questions and I do not propose to do so. What I am discussing is the delays that are occurring in the furnishing of information to the House on matters of importance to the members and to those whom they represent. Yesterday certain questions on the Order Paper were converted into notices of motion, questions, the answers to which could not be brought down in the form of returns, questions that in my opinion should be answered because they relate to the knowledge of the Government with respect to the act of one of their subordinates, the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, Mr. Gutelius. By the action taken, another week or perhaps a fortnight will expire before we can possibly hope to secure this information. I trust my right hon. friend the leader of the Government will call the attention of his Minister of Railways, who is
absent, to the desirability of having all information from the department furnished at the earliest possible moment. I have no desire to complain of lack of courtesy on the part of the Minister of Railways. He takes pride somewhat in the meagreness of the information that he furnishes to the House. Gertainly his friends have rather praised him for the course which he has taken in that regard in times past. In all fairness, I think that we are entitled to this information, and I would rather have it than have a grievance with respect to it. It is a grievance, and I ventilate that grievance in this House on behalf of my constituents, choosing an occasion which is not only opportune but in accordance with the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can assure the hon.
gentleman that the order to which he refers has not been overlooked. But as to there being a serious grievance because he has not been given the information asked for, if he will look at ' Hansard ' he will find questions intended to elicit information as to these promotions in Dorchester penitentiary and also the answers to those questions.

The hon. minister
answered the questions promptly, but that answer did not give the information called for by this motion for a return.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will see if there is
anything further.

I desire to say a word, not by way of complaint, but in view of existing circumstances. There will be a discussion in this House on a certain document recently placed on the table and now in the hands of the printer. It is necessary that members of this House should be seized of the fullest information in order to discuss that matter intelligently. I understand from the press that the health of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) not being the best, he desires to go away as soon as possible, in fact, it is said that a date for his leaving has been fixed. I think the Prime Mnister should impress upon him the necessity of giving us this information at least before he leaves; for, of course-and I am not using these words at all by way of a threat-the Prime Min-

ister will see how impossible it would be for the Minister of Railways to go on with his Estimates until we get the information necessary to discuss this bigger question. I have several questions on the Order Paper, the answers to which should not be very lengthy and the information to answer which, I should think, must be in the Department of Railways here or in the Ottawa office of the Transcontinental Commission. Even if it were more difficult to obtain the information, I think a special effort should be made to answer these questions with all possible speed.

Reference has
just been made by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) to the fact that the Minister of Railways was about to leave Canada for the benefit of his health. That reminds me that the Minister has not yet asked for Supply. There are several matters which I should like to have the
