speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY INVESTIGATING COMMISSION REPORT.
speechtext:
I could not say at the
moment whether that would be possible or not As the minister is going away for a considerable time, there are naturally a great many matters to engage his attention. Whether he will be able to take up Supply or not is unknown to me at the present moment. Of course my hon. friend will understand that if the minister is not here to discuss matters and give information, there will be someone else in his place to perform that duty in the House.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Canada's proportion of expenditure in connection with International Customs Tariffs Bureau, $662.

This is an international
arrangement into which almost all the countries of the world have entered. The head office is located in Brussels. It is an international clearing house for customs tariffs. All the tariffs of the world are collected there and are printed and distributed to all the nations in certain proportions. All changes that take place from time to time are notified there, and notifications are sent out to the different countries. It is a sort of international customs clearing house.
Trade Commissioners and Commercial Agents, including expenses in connection with negotiations of treaties or in extension of commercial relations; miscellaneous advertising and printing, or other expenditure connected with the extension of Canadian trade, $idU,000.
How many trade commissioners have we?

We have at the present
time about fifteen trade commissioners and four correspondents. The trade commissioners are stationed at Leeds, Manchester, Bristol, Birmingham and London in England, and at Glasgow in Scotland. There are trade commissioners, in Paris, at Hamburg, and at Rotterdam. There is a trade commissioner in the West Indies stationed at Barbados, one in South America stationed at Buenos Ayres, and one in 58
China and one in Japan There is also a travelling trade commissioner for the present travelling through the different West Indian islands on a special trade mission. There is a trade commissioner in South Africa, one in Australia ^nd one in New Zealand. I think these take in practically all. We had a trade commissioner in Mexico, but owing to the disjointed state of affairs there that office has been practically closed. Not closed as regards information that may be sought and given, but it is in the hands of the British Trade Consul at that place, who acts under an arrangement with the Foreign Office for Canada with respect to that country. As to the United States, we have no trade commissioners.

Outside of the
commissioner at Barbados, have we not representatives of some kind in the other West Indies, such as Trinidad and Jamaica?
The others are correspondents. They are stationed at Trinidad, the Bahamas, Jamaica, and an acting Trade Commissioner in Havana.
What do you pay these correspondents' ?
I think $500 a year.
What do you pay the trade commissioners ?
They are graded from $3,000 up to $4,000 according to their services and the position, their salaries increasing at the rate of $100 a year.
Where is most of this $150,000 expended ?

It is distributed among the different commissioners I have named. There is the salary of the commissioner, the rent of the commissioner's office, and such clerical assistance as may be employed, and the general expenses of each office. The expenditure as a proportion can be seen when divided amongst the number of trade commissioners.
Was not a commercial agent appointed at Boston two years ago ?

No. I have had a great many requests for the appointment of commissioners in the United States, but we have not appointed any there up to the present time, and it is not the policy of the department to appoint agents there. We have agents in Great Britain for very



good reasons. Then we have agents in foreign countries where we are trying to work up trade and where difficulties, for various reasons, have to be overcome. Our trade with the United States is very large, very free; we are countries which lie in juxtaposition with each other, communication backwards and forwards is of the very best, and I have not thought it necessary to incur the expense of establishing agents in the United States.

Has the minister had any request for the appointment of Mr. Watson Griffin as a special Trade Commissioner to the West Indies? He was appointed a month or two ago at a salary of about $4,000. Has he had any request from any of the exporters in Canada for such an appointment and does he expect that Mr. Griffin can accomplish anything for Canadian trade; and if he thinks so, would he mind telling the committee how? The reason I ask the minister that question, is because I have heard the appointment very severely criticised and I am inclined to think there is nothing which Mr. Griffin can accomplish for our trade in the West Indies. I am not saying anything against Mr. Griffin, I know nothing about him. He may have every accomplishment necessary to make a successful trade commissioner, but really I fail to see what it is he can do for Canadian trade especially in view of the fact that we have correspondents in all those islands who understand the trade very much better than Mr. Griffin can do for a good number of years at least, and who I think are doing everything possible for the extension of our trade with the West Indies. There is also this to be remembered. A great number of Canadian exporters frequently visit the West Indies. It is an old established trade, and is known pretty well.

I will try, I will not say to satisfy my hon. friend, but I will make an explanation with reference to Mr. Griffin's appointment. In the first place, that appointment was not even eolourably made for the sake of finding a billet for a political friend. I think my hon. friend will believe that when I state it to him. I see he assents with a nod and a smile. The West Indian Islands are so situated that it is rather a difficult matter to know what is best to be done in order to bring about the best results. My hon. friend has said that we have commissioners there now. That is true. We have one situated at Barbados, and then we have

three or four correspondents whom we pay at the rate of $500 a year. They do their occasional work but of course they are not supposed to-they could not ibe supposed to-give the whole of their time or a great deal of their effort towards helping trade between the two countries. The islands are very far apart in some respects, and the resident commissioner on one of the islands is, for that island in which he is resident, of some use, but for the islands outside, if he remains resident in the one in which he is placed, he is not of much more use than if he were here in the department at Ottawa. I may say frankly to my hon. friend that the appointment of Mr. Griffin as a special commissioner has been made for a term of one year, is to test out what I am thinking at the present time is the best method of carrying on our commissioner business in the West Indies; that is, instead of having resident commissioners, one or two in one or two of the larger islands, a travelling , commissioner continually going from one island to another with correspondents in the different islands will be, I think, a better solution of the question which we are trying to solve, and will bring better results than any other system that we could have. It was with that in view, that I appointed Mr. Watson Griffin. The question was asked me as to whether I had numerous requests. I had not. I was looking about for a man who had the qualifications for the purpose for which I needed him. The purpose for which he is needed is two-fold. In the first place he has to grasp the salient points in the trade conditions in the West Indies, and in the next place, to present those to the trade and producing public in Canada. Mr. Watson Griffin has, I think, good qualifications for that business. He has had a long experience in Canadian work, and in all parts of Canada. Mr. Griffin was in charge of the Weekly Herald and Star, Montreal, from 1886 to 1896, and was therefore in a commercial metropolis and had to do very largely with commercial currents, commercial thought, and commercial transactions as reflected in that centre. He left the Star for purposes of travel and general press work, going later to the Daily Star as chief editorial writer from 1898 to 1901, again in much the same currents of trade in the central trade position in Canada. In the service of the Star he was sent to make special examinations into the iron and steel industry in Nova Scotia. I have had the pleasure and the benefit of reading Mr. Griffin's reports

on that industry, and they are as able reports as I have ever seen written, well couched in language, selecting the principal points and using no verbiage or effort on what did not seem to be primary matter- on the whole, as good reports as I have read in reference to that kind of investigation. From 1902 to 1906 he was in the service of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, where he became thoroughly acquainted with the manufacturing industries in this country, what is produced, where it is produced, and the quality and the conditions under which it is produced. In 1912 he went to Brandon as publicity commissioner, and it was whilst he was at Brandon that I got into communication with him and asked him to undertake this work. The range over which Mr. Griffin works cannot, I think, be better shown than in the instructions that were issued to him, and if my hon. friend would like to know what those instructions are I will read them to the committee:
1.	Your appointment runs as Special Trade Commissioner to the West India colonies, where the principal part of your labours will be done. This, of course, includes British Guiana.
2.	If not too inconvenient in the way of . transport, you should also visit other principal
West Indian islands, with the exception of Hayti, looking in upon our office at Havana and going thoroughly into conditions and possibilities with Mr. Quilez.
3.	Special attention should be given, when in Jamaica, ta investigate aiul weigh out the conditions there as between Canadian and United States interests. This, of course, has to be very carefully done-diplomatically in fact, so as not to arouse any antipathies, and above all to be careful not to draw public attention ta that phase of your investigation.
4.	In the Danish Islands, if you visit them, it
would be necessary to note, in addition to other information, particularly methods of transportation.	-
5.	In all colonies which you visit, outside of general conditions governing interchanges between them and Canada special attention should be paid to financial and banking facilities,-
My hon. friend will see what an important bearing that has on the general exchanges between the two countries.
-customs, qualities and styles, both of goods and packages which are required by the customs of the people or habits of trade, facilities for transportation, the conditions as to prices and grades of goods required and customs regulations, with a view to noting carefully any existing hindrances to trade in any of these respects which it may be possible to remedy.
6.	Generally your mission will be to interest these people in Canada and Canadian production and resources and impress them so far as possible with our capacity to fill their wants in the leading staple lines. Particular attention cViould also be paid as regards transporta-
56*
tion facilities and freight rates, to the comparative situation as between Canada and the United States, noting whatever conditions may be possessed by the latter and so far as possible suggesting methods by which these can be offset either entirely or in part.
7.	In visiting the different agencies of the department you will try to make yourself thoroughly acquainted with what is being done in each and note, for our information, what improvements you would consider advisable.
8.	As regards statistical data, you will gather everything that may be useful, especially having regard to such points as are not probably brought out by the general public statistics, in so far as these may be made accessory to an increase of trade.
9.	As regards your intercourse with officials and public bodies, you will have letters of introduction in each of the countries you visit, which are to be used, of course, carefully and with due respect to rank and situation.
10.	As to the advisability of public addresses, you will be governed by what you consider is best in each case. Addresses to boards of trade and commercial bodies are valuable when they are properly conceived and carried out, always bearing in mind to keep the country and its interests to the front. Particular care should be taken in regard to newspaper interviewers and reporters to avoid anything that would commit the Government on one hand, or have even the shadow of interference in regard to home questions and controversial subjects.
11.	You will, of course, keep a careful diary of your movements and make extensive notes therein and favour the department with a running report of your work, reserving the main and special preparation of information for use here on your return.
When Mr. Griffin returns, besides the running reports that come in, he will have another mission to perform, and that is to portray to the public through the press and in other ways the conditions that he found in the West Indian Islands, and, by personal communication as well as by literary work, to bring these things before the people as widely and definitely and luminously as possible. I have received some of these reports already, and I can assure my hon. friend that, as far as they have gone, Mr. Griffin has done very valuable work during the short time he has been there and shapes as though he would do very good work for us during his whole mission.

Does he work
with the British Consular offices as the minister has explained is done elsewhere?

Wherever he goes he has letters to the British consuls or the representatives of Great Britain who are there. There are not many British consuls in the West Indies, but the advice, the counsel, and all the courtesies and influences which bring him into connection with people are freely and generously given to him. He

has letters of introduction to the governors of all the islands, and through these he will get all that is necessary to make him au fait with conditions and persons in the islands.

I am very glad to hear such a favourable recommendation of Mr. Griffin. I know nothing of him personally and I trust he is a promising servant of the Government as the minister leads us to believe. However, I think there is a limit to the extension of Canadian trade in the West Indies and I have always feared that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce had altogether too exalted an idea of the possibilities of extending Canadian trade in the British West Indies and that he was prone to indulge in a somewhat too elaborate and expensive a scheme for the development of this trade. Of course, I would not think of impeaching the motives of the minister. I always consider that it is his desire to extend this trade, but my opinion is that he does not have a true conception of trade possibilities between Canada and the West Indies. After consultation with men who know the West Indian trade better than most men in Canada do, I have received the impression that there is decidedly a limit to trade expansion with the British West Indies. I will perhaps discuss this question a little later, on some other Estimates in the minister's department, particu-. larly those which relate to steamship subsidies. That will perhaps be a more opportune time to discuss this particular matter. However, I suppose, as 'the minister suggests, that no harm can be done by giving Mr. Griffin a trial and possibly some good may come of it. Our trade with the British West Indies after all relates to a few products-sugar as an import and fish, lumber and flour as exports. As far as the fish and lumber trade is concerned, no commercial agent can advance that trade in any respect. It is a long established line of trade, is well known to those who are engaged in it in Canada and I think very little or no assistance could be rendered by any official commercial agency. I doubt if any consular or any commercial agent could increase our import of sugar from the British West Indies. I do not think that the minister would argue that he could. Therefore, the work that is open to a commissioner in the British West Indies is very limited indeed. There is always this to be borne in mind, that Great Britain is after all our competitor in that market. They have splendid lines of transportation, their trade with

the West Indies is now quite old and it is a trade which the British people very well understand. The year before last, the Nova Scotian exporters of fish met very severe competition from British exporters. That frequently happens. With regard to almost all that we produce in Canada and which we might probably sell to the British West Indies, we find that freight rates are more favourable from Great Britain to the West Indies than they are from Canada to the West Indies. After all, our strongest competitor in that market is Great Britain, outside of the United States in one or two articles, such as flour. However at a later time, perhaps I will take up this subject.

I may be a little on the optimistic side, but we have undertaken this work and I think it is better to make a trial and make it quickly and that the machinery which is necessary ought to be put into operation at once so that during the continuance of our present steamship subsidy, which is about four or five years now, we will be able to test out the question. I have better hopes of results than my hon. friend has indicated that he has in what he has said to-night. Before Mr. Griffin went I had a circular letter prepared and we sent out about 2,000 to traders, boards of trade and producers in Canada. I think that from those circular letters we certainly got more than a thousand or twelve hundred *replies, and those replies took up just exactly the practical points that were in these persons' minds as to certain things that might be done with' their products in the West Indies.
Almost without exception, they have expressed their gratification that Mr. Griffin was being sent out. Mr. Griffin took these letters with him; he is working at these things as he goes along, and is sending back reports "which are coming in from day to day. The interest shown in this commis-sionership by the business men themselves is one of the most gratifying things about it.
How will you circulate the reports you receive from Mr. Griffin?
Through our bulletins, and by direct correspondence sometimes.

Does the agent do any actual practical work in the way of putting the manufacturers and merchants of Canada in touch with those who want goods in the West Indies? Suppose he saw a newspaper advertisement in Jamaica, requiring buoys for the harbour, or wanting

steel rails, how would he put that information before the Canadian manufacturers? I understand that the agents of the United States Government do practical work of that kind. They do not depend on bulletins, which very few people read.

Our agent would give to
the persons in the West Indian Islands the names of the makers in Canada of any article that would be required, and he would give the same information to the department which publishes the inquiries from week to week in the bulletin. A manufacturer reading that inquiry would communicate with the department, and get the names of the intending purchasers.

If Mr. Griffin
could work out a method of furnishing us with the trade returns by separate islands in the British West Indies, it would be valuable information. I had some difficulty in getting such information last year when our arrangement with the West India Islands was under discussion. Has any of the British West India Islands become a party to the treaty, other than the ten original signatories?

One other island sent
its adherence to the treaty some two or three months aftexwards.
When Mr. Griffin returns will he be available for consultation by manufacturers ?

That is one-half of his
work.

I commend the minister for allowing the trade commissioner to be consulted by the various manufacturers. I know that a great many manufacturers do read the bulletin and that there is a good deal of interest taken in it.

I assume that Jamaica has not so far come into the group of islands which give us a lower rate of duty. Mr. Griffin would confer a great benefit on the producers of pickled fish if he could arrange with the authorities in Jamaica to allow pickled fish to enter that colony free of the import duty, which at present is very heavy. It would be a great boon to the country if pickled fish were allowed into Jamaica at a reasonable rate of duty, if not free of duty altogether. The freight on pickled fish, from Halifax to Jamaica, is three shillings per barrel, and the duty is two and sixpence, so that there is a first charge of $1.50 on the value of the fish, which would be about three dollars per barrel. There was an overstock of alewives last year, and they might have been marketed to more advantage if they were admitted into Jamaica free of duty. Could the minister find out from his agents, the islands into which pickled fish, known as alewives, are imported. The New Brunswick exporters sometimes deliver these fish in New York, and the New York export merchant seems to be able to find a market for them which the Canadian producer cannot overtake. I know there is a considerable market in Hayti for pickled alewives. but except Hayti and Jamaica, I am not aware of any of the British West India Islands which use this fish to any great extent. The same remarks would apply to pickled herrings.

My hon. friend is aware
that Jamaica has not given a preference to Canada, although we give a preierence to her goods.
I am aware of that.

There is a three years'
period of grace allowed, and it is to be hoped that something may eventuate during that time. Of course, the men who export pickled alewives will have to use business methods to find a market, but the aim of the department is to assist them in every way possible by securing whatever information can possibly be obtained to enable them to transact their business. It is difficult to get the statistics the hon. member (Mr. Maclean) has referred to, but we are trying to ascertain as nearly as possible what proportion of Canadian goods comes into these different West India Islands from New York, mainly, and from Boston partly.
If we can differentiate as to that, we can have a much clearer idea of what business we really are doing with the West Indian Islands. That I think can be, although not wholly, approximately brought about. The other is to get the trade statistics of the different islands. Tnese we are getting, but there again we find some difficulty because of the very fact that I have mentioned, of finding out in the different islands the origin of the goods, the place from which they start, a good deal of the importations being through New York and some through Boston. Both of these points are being taken into consideration by the department.

I notice in the Canada West India magazine reference to the matter of shipments of flour which are entitled to preferential treatment under

the West Indian trade agreement. Two shipments from United States ports of what was alleged to be Canadian flour hut which the Comptroller of Customs suspected to be American flour, were the subject of some litigation in the courts of one of the West India Islands. I have observed elsewhere in the press that on one or two other occasions some questions arose as to the validity of certificates of origin of flour shipments entitled to the preferential tariff. One can quite well understand how that difficulty might arise very frequently, particularly in the matter of flour, and one can as well understand that a great deal of American flour might go into the West Indies if improperly invoiced and thus secure the preferential tariff rate.

That was absolutely
liable to take place the moment that the preferential arrangement went into force. It is of course to the interest of Canada that Canadian flour only shall have the preference when it goes into the West Indian Market. Therefore, we are interested in tracing any transactions of that kind or any frauds, if fraud is necessary in order to complete such a transaction. We are following up that matter very carefully in Canada itself. Of course British Guiana and the other colonies-it was in British Guiana where this arose that is alluded to by my hon. friend -are equally interested, in a double capacity. They do not want other than flour which is designated by the treaty to come in under the preference, because of the treaty itself and because of the mutual advantages between the two countries. Also they have a direct interest in the Customs side of it, the revenue side of it, and they are following the matter with very great closeness. The certificates of origin came to the collector in such a way that he did not believe that they were genuine, and on his own belief in the matter he refused to grant the preference and exacted the full duty. He has not been upheld in that. The court by which it was decided took the ground that it must not be simply the belief of the Customs official but that this must be decided by documents. That then brought about what was the natural result: if the present regulations of the Customs are not sufficient, then they will make regulations which they think will be sufficient. New and more stringent regulations have been made, and they require now not only the certificate of origin, but that when ship-

ments pass through New York they shall be visited and attested to by the British Consul in that city.
That is what you would call the continuous bill of lading certified to?

Yes. Then there may be through the railways here a plan worked out which will still more effectually guard it; but if all other things fail, so far as I can judge, the idea of British Guiana, if not of others of the West India Islands, will be to refuse the preference to any flour that does not come by direct shipment. That may be the result. Anyway, the Customs authorities in Barbados and British Guiana are determined that the treaty in its essentials shall be carried out.

It appears to me that
the system which my hon. friend has partly inaugurated, of having these various trade commissioners visit this country at stated times and come into touch with the manufacturers and merchants, is a most excellent one. It is the only way in which trade can be stimulated. I think it would be a good idea, if the period is not too long, if these trade commissioners would spend six months of the year in the country in which they are stationed and the other six months in the Dominion of Canada. In that way the department would be spending its money very wisely. I think the minister said that reams of correspondence came from these trade commissioners to the manufacturers here, and that it was filed and nothing much more heard of it. If that is so, the only way to get over the difficulty and to stimulate trade is to have these commissioners interview the merchants and manufacturers here and in a five minute or a half-hour conversation they might do more than in a month's correspondence. I would urge upon the minister that for 'at least three months of every year these agents should come to the Dominion of Canada from their various stations; that they should get into actual touch with the merchants and manufacturers here. By carrying out a systematic course of visits by these commissioners, trade would be greatly stimulated, which, of course, would be for the benefit of every one.

I think that I mentioned that matter the other day. I would not go
so .far as saying six months and six months because I think that one-fourth of the time here and three-fourths in the foreign or

outside country would be a fairer proportion.
Perhaps so. .

Immediately after I came into connection with this. I saw that a great deal of expenditure and effort was lost because it did not get the application to the business men in our own country.
It is a policy that I have adopted and will carry out, that a certain proportion of the time of each year will be spent in Canada by the trade commissioners. As an example of that, Mr. Poussette made a very thorough tour of the whole of South America and went into every country. He had the best facilities for gaining knowledge; talked with the best businessmen in South America. He then came back, and has been two months in this country, going through to British Columbia, and will be here another month. The information I get from him is that his work here has been more satisfactory than two years' work at long distance would have been. He has brought men together. Having made these personal visits in the other countries, making the personal visit here to the man who is interested, he is able to bring together for business men whom he probably never could have brought together by correspondence. I thoroughly believe that a portion of the vote should be spent on home mission work as well as the other portion on foreign mission work.

If this is the proper time,
I should like to ask what pro-11 p.m. gxess is being made in trade with Japan. What articles are we sending to Japan, and is our trade wiuh that country increasing or decreasing?

I have not the report for this year with me, and therefore my answer will be general. Our trade with Japan is increasing, and during the past year there was, I think, an increase in the quantity of flour we sold to that country. I think I made the remark somewhere that there were promises in the East of consumption of Canadian grain material which we_ could not afford to overlook. I think China is naturally one of the richest countries in the world, yet, so far as its resources are concerned, except in agriculture, it is one of the least developed of the great countries in the world. One cause of lack of development has been the lack of internal communication; you cannot do much m
trdde over a vast area if you have to carry everything in baskets slung over your shoulder along footpaths in which even an animal would find ^ it difficult to keep its tracks. But China is growing in the way of railroad expansion, and when once she gets railway facilities her development will be very great indeed. That is going to do two things.
In the first place it is going to open up the whole country to western ideas, new activities, and customs of living. In the second place, it is going to cause a very large demand for machinery, for workmen's tools and for all that attaches to development of that kind. The four hundred millions of China and the sixty-five millions of Japan live, as a rule, on scant material. And, although some people may laugh at the idea, the fact is that in Japan and in parts of China rice is becoming too dear for the native to eat. His best grades of rice are sold in the foreign market, and he is restricted to the inferior grades or to something else which does him for food. They are beginning to get the idea of adding the products of flour. Once that idea is taken up, even though there be but a gradual and fractional increase, just compute what the result will be among those hundreds of millions of people. Though the increase be but little in each case or in each district, the aggregate will be enormous. In this respect, I believe that in both China and Japan there is a great future for Canadian flour, wheat and other Canadian products. We have a great front door on the Pacific, and through it look out upon these nationalities which in the future are to be live centres of industry and production, and we cannot afford not to keep our eyes wide open and have every string we possibly can attached to the growing trade of tnose countries.
Do they produce wheat themselves?
To a certain extent. But rice is the main production, with millet, the soya bean, vegetables of every conceivable kind, and roots that grow in all sorts of contorted shapes and in Infinite variety.

Has the hon. minister any plan to teach the Chinaman to abandon rice and eat Canadian flour? We have heard that it is extremely difficult to turn the Chinaman's mind towards anything new. We all remember Charles Lamb's story of how the Chinaman com

menced to eat roast pork. The House of one of them got afire, and as the pig was living in the House, he was burnt. In clearing up the ashes, the owner got his fingers into the carcase of the pig, and, putting them into his mouth, got the first taste any Chinaman had had of roast pork. Then, they began setting fire to their houses everywhere to enjoy this new dainty. Finally, a great philosopher arose who told them that they could roast pork without burning down their houses. Has the minister any method by which he can do the trick of causing the Chinaman to use flour instead of rice?

The minister has told us what is possible, but I was anxious to know what was being done and how far we had progressed in the sale of flour, fish lumber and other things to Japan. What is the amount of our trade there, approximately? Do we find in China and Japan parallel conditions to those existing in the West Indies-that our competitors to the south have established themselves in the trade of these countries, and we not only have the difficulty of bringing our products to the favourable attention of the people hut also have, to a certain extent, to displace some of our competitors m order to attain these markets. How much flour are we selling to Japan to-day and how much is the United States selling I would like the same information in regard

As I said I have not the reports before me for the year and I cannot carry these in my head, but if the hon. member will look at part No. 3 of the report of my department he will find that information extended in detail for a period of years. Offhand, the trade with Japan is increasing substantially. Our exports to Japan and China are also increasing. I know from having visited that country

that in the matter of flour and lumber, but partially of flour, we are already doing quite a trade with China.

Mr. OLIVER The newspapers published sometime ago a statement that our flour was displacing that of the United States in the Chinese markets. That is a very satisfactory condition of affairs. Has the minister information to that effect, that our flour, on account of its superior quality, was displacing the flour of the United States in the markets of China?

Whether it is displacing
it or finding greater access without displacing United States flour I cannot say without looking at the statistics, but I can say it is going into China in increased quantities. It is not altogether the superior quality of flour that is looked for by either Japanese or Chinese; they do not take the highest grade of flour, and it is a competition in the lower grades of flour. That is one of the best competitions for Canadian millers, as my hon. friend will see. They have no difficulty in getting rid of their high grade flour in this country, the difficulty is to find markets for the low grade flour.
Does the information received show whether the bulk of this flour is consumed by the common people or by the better classes?

The sale of flour as of
most products in China is not, in the first place, to the masses of the people, it is to what they call the different guilds and the negotiations must be conducted and any arrangement must be made with the guild. Once you get a large and prominent guild interested in your quality or brand of flour and they take it, your work is done, they do all the distributing, as to who eats that flour after it gets in, I think it is distributed probably a little generally; but the lower grades would go to the lower classes of the people and the higher grades to the better classes of Chinese, much the same as it would here.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks which the hon. member for West Lambton, (Mr. Pardee) has just made are very important and very wise. There is no doubt that the taade commissioners who represent our country abroad cannot render the same services to us as they would *be able to do if they were well acquainted with our resources, and they could acquaint themselves with them by visiting our coun-

try every year, by communicating with our business men, instead of merely sending in reports, as they do.
I would like to know from toe Minister of Trade and Commerce the average salary of these commissioners in England, Rotterdam and Hamburg.

I have stated that the
salaries grade from $3,000 a year to $4,000, according to years of service. The commissioner at Hamburg is a new appointment, and he receives $3,000. At Rotterdam the commissioner, who is an older servant of the department appointed in 1910, receives a larger salary and so on, according to the service that has been given the salary grades.
As I unaerstand the list, we have no such commissioner in France, Italy, Spain or Germany?

We have a trade commissioner in Paris, who is one of the highest paid trade commissioners in the service. His duties are primarily to look after tit! extension of trade, seek information, answer inquiries and communicate with the-department. We have no other trade commissioner in France except that general trade commissioner in Paris. In Italy we have had no trade commissioner as, indeed, we have not had trade commissioners in most of the the European countries. That service is being gradually extended and I have not tried to extend it much because I have not been certain that the work is being carried on on the proper basis. We have spent a good deal of money, and I am afraid we have not received the best results. I am going slowly in order to work out the best plan for doing it before extending very largely into other countries. But I was successful in making an arrangement with the Foreign Office, through the Colonial office, by which the British consular trade agents, wherever we wish them, will act for Canada the same as our trade commissioners do, in the way of receiving letters of inquiry and giving information as to openings for Canadian trade. While always they must consider that their first duty is to British trade, they are asked and instructed to answer such inquiries and give such information. I suppose there never has been a time when a British trade consul has not been willing to do that, but they have never before been given to understand that that -was a part of their duty, and Canada never before felt that she had a right to ask them. Under that arrangement
1 am arranging to-day for the British representatives at Milan and Genoa and perhaps another city in Italy to represent Canada in those places. The same thing is being done in the different European and some Asiatic countries where we have now some trade, and as the trade develops this arrangement with the British consuls will be brought into effect.

Before this item is passed, I would like to ask the minister a question respecting the tariff upon dried salt fish entering Portugal. This is a matter of some interest to the Maritime provinces, as from there quite a quantity of salt fish is shipped. British dried fish entering Portugal pays thirty-five cents per quintal higher than fish from Norway, Germany, or Iceland. Canadian exporters of dried salt fish feel this additional tariff to be quite an impediment to their trade. I mention this to the minister because a resolution respecting it was passed by the Halifax Board of Trade, and a copy of it sent to the minister for his consideration,, at a time when I think a new commercial treaty was being negotiated between Great Britain and Portugal. Perhaps the minister can tell us whether he has had it under consideration.

Yes. Great Britain has,
for the last two years, been trying to negotiate a treaty with Portugal. It has not yet been negotiated. When I was in London, I saw the representatives of the foreign office and of the colonial office and discussed the matter with them, and the British Government has that matter in charge for us. The whole matter has been placed before them. Of course, Portugal will naturally require a quid pro quo from Great Britain if such a treaty is finally brought to a fulfilment, and a quid pro quo will naturally be required from Canada, for instance, should she get her fish in on a favoured basis. In the ultimate result it will depend on what the quid pro quo is
I would like to know what progress our trade is making with Australia and New Zealand: what lines of produce we are sending in, and particularly what we are getting?

In regard to Australia, the trade is increasing each year. We have no preferential arrangement with Australia. We send to Australia even under present conditions, a large amount of print paper, automobiles and vehicles of that kind to a large extent. We send lumber

to a certain extent, and a lot of manufactured articles spread over quite a large range. Then our natural productions such as apples are sent over. The two seasons are the exact opposites of each other. When they have no fresh fruit, ours is in season and vice versa, and there is the foundation of a fairly good trade, I think.
Do we ship any considerable quantity of apples to Australia?
The apple trade is growing. I think quite a considerable quantity is being sent there; certainly a considerable quantity is being shipped to New Zealand and the trade is growing quite rapidly.
Are they British Columbia apples or eastern apples.

I think largely British Columbia apples, because they are close to the coast and are shipped at much less expense than apples from this side can be shipped. Australia sends to us a certain quantity of dried fruit. Part of Australia is a grape growing country. When in Australia, I visited the warehouses of producers and sellers, who were at that time shipping quite a large quantity of dried fruits, raisins and things of that sort as far east as Winnipeg, and, as they informed me, were making a fairly good trade. They also send to us meat and butter and some few other products. The increase in trade between New Zealand and Canada has been very marked on both sides. Our exports to that country have increased largely, and their exports to us in the lines of butter and meats have also increased largely. There is quite a difference between Australia and New Zealand. In the first place, we have a preference with New Zealand and not with Australia; but there is another difference still more important, and that is, New Zealand manufactures to only a very small degree. The result is that quite a large range of manufactured articles are going from this country to New Zealand, and in increasing quantities. When I was in New Zealand, I met travellers from St. Catherines and other places in Ontario who were travelling in that country, and who told me they had been more successful in placing orders than they anticipated.
Do we send a considerable quantity of agricultural implements to Australia and New Zealand ?

Yes, the agricultural implements of Canada take the field in Australia and New Zealand. We send a great

number of reapers to those countries. Canadian automobiles also are shipped to a very large extent and paper is exported to a large extent. In fact, we are taking quite largely the paper trade of South Africa, New Zealand and Australia.
